qa_pairs.question: What is the legal definition of theft of services and how does it apply to someone leaving a restaurant without paying for their meal?
qa_pairs.answer: Theft of services is legally defined as the act of availing oneself of the services of another without paying for them. This is considered a crime in most states. A common example of this is when someone leaves a restaurant without paying for their meal. In such cases, the person is guilty of theft of services because they have taken advantage of the restaurant's services without providing the agreed-upon compensation. The statutes specifically define this act as theft of services, making it a punishable offense.

qa_pairs.question: What constitutes forgery and how does it differ from uttering a forged instrument?
qa_pairs.answer: Forgery is the false writing of a document of legal significance with the intent to defraud. It includes the creation of a false document or the alteration of an existing one. The forged document must be false, not merely contain a falsehood. Forgery can be committed by typing, printing, or any other means. Common subjects of forgery include negotiable instruments, deeds, receipts, contracts, and bills of lading. Uttering, or presenting, a forged instrument is also unlawful, regardless of whether the person uttering it actually forged it. The key difference between forgery and uttering a forged instrument is that forgery involves the creation or alteration of a false document, while uttering involves presenting or using a forged document with the intent to defraud.

Bribery 
Bribery is a corrupt payment (or receipt of such a payment) for official action. The payment can be in 
cash or in the form of any goods, intangibles, or services that the recipient would find valuable. Under 
common law, only a public official could be bribed. In most states, bribery charges can result from the 
bribe of anyone performing a public function. 
 
Bribing a public official in government procurement (contracting) can result in serious criminal charges. 
Bribing a public official in a foreign country to win a contract can result in charges under the Foreign 
Corrupt Practices Act. 
 
Perjury 
Perjury is the crime of giving a false oath, either orally or in writing, in a judicial or other official 
proceeding (lies made in proceedings other than courts are sometimes termed “false swearing”). To be 
perjurious, the oath must have been made corruptly—that is, with knowledge that it was false or without 
sincere belief that it was true. An innocent mistake is not perjury. A statement, though true, is perjury if

the maker of it believes it to be false. Statements such as “I don’t remember” or “to the best of my 
knowledge” are not sufficient to protect a person who is lying from conviction for perjury. To support a 
charge of perjury, however, the false statement must be “material,” meaning that the statement is relevant 
to whatever the court is trying to find out. 
 
White-Collar Crime 
White-collar crime, as distinguished from “street crime,” refers generally to fraud-related acts carried 
out in a nonviolent way, usually connected with business. Armed bank robbery is not a white-collar crime, 
but embezzlement by a teller or bank officer is. Many white-collar crimes are included within the statutory 
definitions of embezzlement and false pretenses. Most are violations of state law. Depending on how they 
are carried out, many of these same crimes are also violations of federal law. 
 
Any act of fraud in which the United States postal system is used or which involves interstate phone calls 
or Internet connections is a violation of federal law. Likewise, many different acts around the buying and 
selling of securities can run afoul of federal securities laws. Other white-collar crimes include tax fraud; 
price fixing; violations of food, drug, and environmental laws; corporate bribery of foreign companies; 
and—the newest form—computer fraud. Some of these are discussed here; others are covered in later 
chapters.

Mail and Wire Fraud 
Federal law prohibits the use of the mails or any interstate electronic communications medium for the 
purpose of furthering a “scheme or artifice to defraud.” The statute is broad, and it is relatively easy for 
prosecutors to prove a violation. The law also bans attempts to defraud, so the prosecutor need not show 
that the scheme worked or that anyone suffered any losses. “Fraud” is broadly construed: anyone who 
uses the mails or telephone to defraud anyone else of virtually anything, not just of money, can be 
convicted under the law. In one case, a state governor was convicted of mail fraud when he took bribes to 
influence the setting of racing dates. The court’s theory was that he defrauded the citizenry of its right to 
his “honest and faithful services” as governor. [1]

Violations of the Food and Drug Act 
The federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act prohibits any person or corporation from sending into 
interstate commerce any adulterated or misbranded food, drug, cosmetics, or related device. For example, 
in a 2010 case, Allergen had to pay a criminal fine for marketing Botox as a headache or pain reliever, a 
use that had not been approved by the Food and Drug Administration. Unlike most criminal statutes, 
willfulness or deliberate misconduct is not an element of the act. As the United States v. Park case 
(Section 6.7 "Cases") shows, an executive can be held criminally liable even though he may have had no 
personal knowledge of the violation.

As a byproduct of Watergate, federal officials at the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Internal 
Revenue Service uncovered many instances of bribes paid by major corporations to officials of foreign 
governments to win contracts with those governments. Congress responded in 1977 with the Foreign 
Corrupt Practices Act, which imposed a stringent requirement that the disposition of assets be accurately

In 1970 Congress enacted the Racketeering Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO), aimed at

broadly “to effectuate its remedial purpose,” and many who are not part of organized crime have been

least two acts within ten years of any of a variety of already-existing crimes, including mail, wire, and 
securities fraud. The act thus makes many types of fraud subject to severe penalties.

qa_pairs.question: What is the purpose of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and what activities does it prohibit?
qa_pairs.answer: The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) was enacted in 1977 in response to instances of bribery by major corporations to foreign government officials to secure contracts. The primary purpose of the FCPA is to ensure that the disposition of assets is accurately and fairly accounted for in a company's books and records. The Act makes it illegal to pay bribes to foreign officials or to anyone who will transmit the money to a foreign official to assist in obtaining business. This legislation aims to prevent corruption and promote fair business practices in international dealings. By prohibiting such corrupt activities, the FCPA seeks to maintain the integrity of the global business environment and ensure that contracts are awarded based on merit rather than illicit payments.

qa_pairs.question: What is the main federal statutory framework for many computer crimes, and what are the penalties for obtaining national security information under this act?
qa_pairs.answer: The main federal statutory framework for many computer crimes is the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA). Under this act, obtaining national security information can result in severe penalties. Specifically, Section (a)(1) of the CFAA stipulates that obtaining national security information can lead to a maximum sentence of 10 years, which can increase to 20 years for a second offense. This framework was established to protect federal interests, particularly when government computers are involved or when the crime has an interstate nature.

qa_pairs.question: How does the CFAA define and penalize trespassing in a government computer, and what are the potential consequences for compromising the confidentiality of a computer?
qa_pairs.answer: The CFAA defines trespassing in a government computer under Section (a)(3) and penalizes it with a sentence of up to 1 year, which can increase to 5 years under certain conditions. Compromising the confidentiality of a computer is addressed in Section (a)(2) of the CFAA, with penalties ranging from 1 year to 10 years, depending on the severity and circumstances of the offense. These provisions are designed to protect the integrity and confidentiality of government and other sensitive computer systems from unauthorized access and exploitation.

To be guilty of a crime, you must have acted. Mental desire or intent to do so is insufficient. But what 
constitutes an act? This question becomes important when someone begins to commit a crime, or 
does so in association with others, or intends to do one thing but winds up doing something else. 
 
Attempt 
It is not necessary to commit the intended crime to be found guilty of a criminal offense. An attempt to 
commit the crime is punishable as well, though usually not as severely. For example, Brett points a gun at 
Ashley, intending to shoot her dead. He pulls the trigger but his aim is off, and he misses her heart by four 
feet. He is guilty of an attempt to murder. Suppose, however, that earlier in the day, when he was 
preparing to shoot Ashley, Brett had been overheard in his apartment muttering to himself of his 
intention, and that a neighbor called the police. When they arrived, he was just snapping his gun into his 
shoulder holster. 
 
At that point, courts in most states would not consider him guilty of an attempt because he had not passed 
beyond the stage of preparation. After having buttoned his jacket he might have reconsidered and put the 
gun away. Determining when the accused has passed beyond mere preparation and taken an actual step 
toward perpetrating the crime is often difficult and is usually for the jury to decide. 
 
Impossibility 
What if a defendant is accused of attempting a crime that is factually impossible? For example, suppose 
that men believed they were raping a drunken, unconscious woman, and were later accused of attempted 
rape, but defended on the grounds of factual impossibility because the woman was actually dead at the 
time sexual intercourse took place? Or suppose that a husband intended to poison his wife with

qa_pairs.question: What is the significance of intention in criminal law and criminal prosecutions, and how does it affect the determination of guilt?
qa_pairs.answer: In criminal law, intention plays a crucial role in determining guilt. For an individual to be found guilty of a crime, there must be evidence of both the act (actus reus) and the mental state (mens rea) at the time the crime was committed. Intention refers to the mental desire or intent to commit a crime, which is a necessary component for establishing criminal liability. However, merely having the intention to commit a crime is not sufficient for a conviction. The law requires that the individual must have taken a substantial step towards committing the crime, demonstrating that they moved beyond mere preparation and towards perpetration. This distinction is important because it helps to differentiate between someone who has merely thought about committing a crime and someone who has taken concrete actions towards its commission. The determination of whether an individual has crossed the line from preparation to attempt is often complex and is typically left to the discretion of a jury. The jury must consider the actions of the accused and the circumstances surrounding those actions to decide if they constitute an attempt to commit the crime. This assessment involves evaluating whether the accused's actions were a clear step towards the commission of the crime, even if the crime was not ultimately completed. The concept of intention in criminal law underscores the importance of both the mental and physical elements of a crime, ensuring that individuals are held accountable for their actions and intentions.

qa_pairs.question: How can a corporation be held criminally liable for the actions of its agents, and what are the implications of this for corporate governance?
qa_pairs.answer: A corporation can be held criminally liable for the actions of its agents through the legal doctrine of vicarious liability, which holds that a corporation can be responsible for the criminal acts committed by its employees or agents if those acts were performed within the scope of their employment or authority. This means that if an employee or agent of a corporation commits a crime while carrying out their job duties, the corporation itself can be held accountable for the crime. The rationale behind this principle is that corporations, as legal entities, have the power to control and direct the actions of their employees, and therefore, they should bear the responsibility for ensuring that their agents act lawfully. The implications of this for corporate governance are significant. Corporations must implement robust compliance programs, conduct thorough background checks, provide adequate training, and establish clear policies and procedures to prevent criminal behavior by their employees. Additionally, corporations must foster a culture of ethical behavior and accountability, ensuring that employees understand the legal and moral implications of their actions. Failure to do so can result in severe penalties, including fines, sanctions, and reputational damage. By holding corporations accountable for the actions of their agents, the law aims to promote responsible corporate behavior and deter criminal conduct within the business community.

Conspiracy 
Under both federal and state laws, it is a separate offense to work with others toward the commission of a 
crime. When two or more people combine to carry out an unlawful purpose, they are engaged in a 
conspiracy. The law of conspiracy is quite broad, especially when it is used by prosecutors in connection 
with white-collar crimes. Many people can be swept up in the net of conspiracy, because it is unnecessary 
to show that the actions they took were sufficient to constitute either the crime or an attempt. Usually, the 
prosecution needs to show only (1) an agreement and (2) a single overt act in furtherance of the 
conspiracy. Thus if three people agree to rob a bank, and if one of them goes to a store to purchase a gun 
to be used in the holdup, the three can be convicted of conspiracy to commit robbery. Even the purchase 
of an automobile to be used as the getaway car could support a conspiracy conviction. 
 
The act of any one of the conspirators is imputed to the other members of the conspiracy. It does not 
matter, for instance, that only one of the bank robbers fired the gun that killed a guard. All can be 
convicted of murder. That is so even if one of the conspirators was stationed as a lookout several blocks 
away and even if he specifically told the others that his agreement to cooperate would end “just as soon as 
there is shooting.”

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between factual impossibility and legal impossibility as defenses in criminal law?
qa_pairs.answer: Factual impossibility occurs when a defendant's intended actions do not fulfill all the required elements of a crime due to some factual circumstance, such as shooting at a tree stump instead of a person, which many courts would not consider an attempt. Legal impossibility, on the other hand, happens when a defendant completes all the intended acts, but those acts do not constitute a crime because they lack a necessary element of the crime, such as shooting at a tree stump, thinking it is a person, which many courts would acknowledge as a valid defense. The distinction between the two is not always clear, and there is a trend towards punishing the intended attempt regardless of the impossibility.

qa_pairs.question: How does the law of conspiracy work, and what are the requirements for a conviction under federal and state laws?
qa_pairs.answer: The law of conspiracy involves two or more people agreeing to commit an unlawful act and taking steps towards its execution. Under both federal and state laws, conspiracy is a separate offense from the actual commission of the crime. To secure a conviction for conspiracy, the prosecution typically needs to prove only two elements: (1) an agreement between two or more persons to commit a crime, and (2) an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy. This overt act does not need to be sufficient to constitute the crime itself; it merely needs to demonstrate that the conspiracy was in motion. For example, if three individuals agree to rob a bank and one of them purchases a gun for the robbery, they can all be convicted of conspiracy to commit robbery, even if only one person actually fired the gun. The law of conspiracy is particularly broad and is often used in white-collar crime cases, where it can be difficult to prove the actual commission of the crime. The actions of any one conspirator are imputed to the others, meaning that all members of the conspiracy can be held accountable for the actions of their co-conspirators, regardless of their individual roles or intentions.

qa_pairs.question: Can a person be guilty of a crime if they act through another individual, and how does this relate to the concept of conspiracy?
qa_pairs.answer: Yes, a person can be guilty of a crime if they act through another individual, and this concept is closely related to conspiracy. In criminal law, the guilt of an individual can be imputed to another person if both were engaged in a conspiracy. A conspiracy involves an agreement between two or more persons to commit a criminal act. However, imputation of guilt is not limited to conspiracies. For instance, if a corporate officer directs a junior employee to take a bag containing money that belongs to the company, the officer can be held guilty of larceny even if the employee was unaware of the money's origin. The employee's innocence does not absolve the officer of guilt because the officer's intent to keep the money is imputed to him. This principle ensures that individuals cannot escape liability simply by acting through others.

qa_pairs.question: Under what circumstances can a corporation be held criminally liable, and how has the law of corporate criminal responsibility evolved recently?
qa_pairs.answer: A corporation can be held criminally liable under certain circumstances, particularly when the act has been directed by a responsible officer or group within the corporation, such as the president or board of directors. The antitrust statutes explicitly state that a corporation may be convicted and fined for violations committed by its employees. This holds true even if the shareholders, who are ultimately responsible for paying the fines, had no involvement in the crime or the power to prevent it. In recent years, the law of corporate criminal responsibility has evolved to hold corporations more accountable. The trend is to impose liability on corporations if the criminal act was directed by a responsible officer or group within the corporation. This shift aims to ensure that corporations cannot evade criminal responsibility by distancing themselves from the actions of their employees or lower-level managers.

In General 
The mens rea requirement depends on the nature of the crime and all the circumstances surrounding the

mildly ill? The act is still murder, because we are all liable for the consequences of any intentional act that

qa_pairs.question: What is the significance of mens rea in criminal law, and how can it be established?
qa_pairs.answer: Mens rea, or the 'guilty mind,' is a fundamental principle in criminal law that requires the defendant to have a criminal intent or state of mind at the time of committing the act. It is significant because it distinguishes between someone who committed an act accidentally or without intent and someone who did so with a deliberate purpose to cause harm or achieve a criminal outcome. Mens rea can be established directly, through evidence showing the defendant's intent, or indirectly, through inference from the circumstances surrounding the act. For instance, if a person gives another person a poison capsule with the intention of causing harm, the act of giving the capsule itself, combined with the knowledge of its lethal nature, establishes mens rea. However, if the giver believed the capsule to be harmless, despite it being poison, the mens rea might not be established, as there was no intent to cause harm. Courts look at the nature of the crime, the defendant's actions, and the context to determine whether mens rea can be inferred. This principle ensures that individuals are held accountable for their intentional actions and not merely for accidents or unintended consequences.

qa_pairs.question: How can a corporation be held criminally responsible for the actions of its agents or contractors, even if the CEO, board of directors, and shareholders have not personally committed a crime?
qa_pairs.answer: A corporation can be held criminally responsible for the actions of its agents or contractors through the legal doctrine of vicarious liability, which holds that an entity can be liable for the actions of its employees or representatives if those actions were performed within the scope of their employment or agency. This means that if a corporate officer or contractor commits a crime while performing duties related to their role within the corporation, the corporation itself can be held accountable. For example, if a corporate officer instructs a contractor to engage in illegal activities, and the contractor follows through, the corporation may be charged with conspiracy or other criminal offenses. The key factor is whether the criminal act was committed as part of the agent's or contractor's job responsibilities. This principle ensures that corporations cannot evade responsibility for illegal acts committed by individuals acting on their behalf. It also serves as a deterrent, encouraging corporations to implement strict compliance programs and oversight mechanisms to prevent criminal conduct by their employees and contractors.

Excuses That Limit or Overcome Responsibility 
Mistake of Fact and Mistake of Law 
Ordinarily, ignorance of the law is not an excuse. If you believe that it is permissible to turn right on a red 
light but the city ordinance prohibits it, your belief, even if reasonable, does not excuse your violation of 
the law. Under certain circumstances, however, ignorance of law will be excused. If a statute imposes 
criminal penalties for an action taken without a license, and if the government official responsible for 
issuing the license formally tells you that you do not need one (though in fact you do), a conviction for 
violating the statute cannot stand. In rare cases, a lawyer’s advice, contrary to the statute, will be held to 
excuse the client, but usually the client is responsible for his attorney’s mistakes. Otherwise, as it is said, 
the lawyer would be superior to the law. 
 
Ignorance or mistake of fact more frequently will serve as an excuse. If you take a coat from a restaurant,

qa_pairs.question: What is the legal principle that excuses criminal responsibility when a person acts under a mistaken belief of fact, and what are the three conditions that must be met for this principle to apply?
qa_pairs.answer: The legal principle that excuses criminal responsibility when a person acts under a mistaken belief of fact is known as 'mistake of fact'. For this principle to apply, three conditions must be met: (1) the belief must be honestly held by the accused, meaning that the person genuinely believed in the truth of the facts as they perceived them; (2) the belief must be reasonable, indicating that a reasonable person in the same circumstances would have held the same belief; and (3) the act would not have been criminal if the facts were as the accused supposed them to have been. This means that if the accused had known the true facts, their actions would not have constituted a criminal offense. This principle is based on the understanding that criminal liability typically requires a culpable state of mind, and if the accused did not have the requisite intent due to a genuine and reasonable mistake of fact, they should not be held criminally responsible.

qa_pairs.question: Under what circumstances can ignorance of the law be excused, and how does this differ from the treatment of ignorance of fact in criminal law?
qa_pairs.answer: Ignorance of the law is generally not an excuse in criminal law, as it is presumed that individuals are aware of the laws that govern their conduct. However, there are rare circumstances where ignorance of the law can be excused. One such circumstance is when a government official responsible for issuing a license informs the individual that they do not need one, despite the fact that they do. In this case, a conviction for violating the statute cannot stand because the individual was misled by an official authority. Another rare exception is when a lawyer's advice, contrary to the statute, is relied upon by the client, and the lawyer's mistake is held to excuse the client. This is because lawyers are expected to be knowledgeable about the law, and their advice carries weight. In contrast, ignorance of fact is more frequently excused in criminal law. If an individual takes an action based on a mistaken belief of fact, such as taking a coat from a restaurant believing it to be their own, they cannot be convicted of larceny if the mistake is honest, reasonable, and the act would not have been criminal if the facts were as the accused believed them to be. The key difference is that ignorance of fact negates the requisite intent for a crime, while ignorance of the law typically does not, unless specific exceptions apply.

Entrapment 
One common technique of criminal investigation is the use of an undercover agent or decoy—the 
policeman who poses as a buyer of drugs from a street dealer or the elaborate “sting” operations in which 
ostensibly stolen goods are “sold” to underworld “fences.” Sometimes these methods are the only way by 
which certain kinds of crime can be rooted out and convictions secured. 
 
But a rule against entrapment limits the legal ability of the police to play the role of criminals. The 
police are permitted to use such techniques to detect criminal activity; they are not permitted to do so to 
instigate crime. The distinction is usually made between a person who intends to commit a crime and one 
who does not. If the police provide the former with an opportunity to commit a criminal act—the sale of 
drugs to an undercover agent, for example—there is no defense of entrapment. But if the police knock on 
the door of one not known to be a drug user and persist in a demand that he purchase drugs from them, 
finally overcoming his will to resist, a conviction for purchase and possession of drugs can be overturned 
on the ground of entrapment. 
 
Other Excuses 
A number of other circumstances can limit or excuse criminal liability. These include compulsion (a gun 
pointed at one’s head by a masked man who apparently is unafraid to use the weapon and who demands 
that you help him rob a store), honest consent of the “victim” (the quarterback who is tackled), adherence 
to the requirements of legitimate public authority lawfully exercised (a policeman directs a towing 
company to remove a car parked in a tow-away zone), the proper exercise of domestic authority (a parent 
may spank a child, within limits), and defense of self, others, property, and habitation. Each of these 
excuses is a complex subject in itself.

qa_pairs.question: What is entrapment and how does it limit the legal ability of the police to instigate crime?
qa_pairs.answer: Entrapment is a defense in criminal law that limits the legal ability of the police to instigate crime. It occurs when law enforcement officers induce a person to commit a criminal act that they would not have otherwise committed. The distinction between entrapment and legitimate police investigation is crucial. While police are allowed to use undercover agents or decoys to detect criminal activity, they are not permitted to instigate crime. For instance, if an undercover agent poses as a buyer of drugs and persuades a street dealer to sell drugs, there is no defense of entrapment because the dealer intended to commit the crime. However, if the police persistently demand that a person, who is not known to be a drug user, purchase drugs from them, overcoming their will to resist, a conviction for purchase and possession of drugs can be overturned on the grounds of entrapment. The key factor is whether the person was predisposed to commit the crime or was induced by the police to commit it.

qa_pairs.question: What are some of the other circumstances that can limit or excuse criminal liability?
qa_pairs.answer: Several circumstances can limit or excuse criminal liability, including compulsion, honest consent of the 'victim', adherence to legitimate public authority lawfully exercised, proper exercise of domestic authority, and defense of self, others, property, and habitation. Compulsion involves being forced to commit a crime under threat, such as being threatened with a gun. Honest consent of the 'victim' refers to situations where the person being harmed consents to the act, such as a quarterback being tackled during a game. Adherence to legitimate public authority lawfully exercised means following lawful orders from public officials, like a policeman directing a towing company to remove a car from a tow-away zone. Proper exercise of domestic authority refers to actions taken by parents within reasonable limits, such as spanking a child. Defense of self, others, property, and habitation involves protecting oneself, others, property, or one's home from harm. Each of these excuses is a complex subject and can vary in application depending on the circumstances.

LEARNING OBJECTIVES 
 
1. Describe the basic steps in pretrial criminal procedure that follow a government's determination to arrest 
someone for an alleged criminal act. 
2. Describe the basic elements of trial and posttrial criminal procedure. 
 
 
The procedure for criminal prosecutions is complex. Procedures will vary from state to state. A 
criminal case begins with an arrest if the defendant is caught in the act or fleeing from the scene; if 
the defendant is not caught, a warrant for the defendant’s arrest will issue. The warrant is issued by a 
judge or a magistrate upon receiving a complaint detailing the charge of a specific crime against the 
accused. It is not enough for a police officer to go before a judge and say, “I’d like you to arrest 
Bonnie because I think she’s just murdered Clyde.” She must supply enough information to satisfy 
the magistrate that there is probable cause (reasonable grounds) to believe that the accused 
committed the crime. The warrant will be issued to any officer or agency that has power to arrest the 
accused with warrant in hand. 
 
The accused will be brought before the magistrate for a preliminary hearing. The purpose of the 
hearing is to determine whether there is sufficient reason to hold the accused for trial. If so, the 
accused can be sent to jail or be permitted to make bail. Bail is a sum of money paid to the court to 
secure the defendant’s attendance at trial. If he fails to appear, he forfeits the money.

qa_pairs.question: What is the purpose of a preliminary hearing in the criminal procedure, and what can happen if the accused fails to appear for it?
qa_pairs.answer: The purpose of a preliminary hearing in the criminal procedure is to determine whether there is sufficient reason to hold the accused for trial. During this hearing, the court assesses the evidence presented by the prosecution to decide if there is probable cause to believe that the accused committed the crime. If the court finds that there is enough evidence to proceed, the accused can be sent to jail or be permitted to make bail. Bail is a sum of money paid to the court to secure the defendant’s attendance at trial. If the accused fails to appear for the trial after being released on bail, they forfeit the bail money and may face additional legal consequences.

qa_pairs.question: How does the concept of 'lack of capacity' function as a defense in criminal law, and under what circumstances might it be considered by the courts?
qa_pairs.answer: The concept of 'lack of capacity' functions as a defense in criminal law by arguing that the accused was not mentally capable of understanding the nature of their actions or distinguishing right from wrong at the time of the crime. This defense is often invoked in cases involving mental illness, insanity, or intoxication. However, the mere fact of drunkenness is not ordinarily sufficient to establish lack of capacity. The courts will consider this defense when there is substantial evidence that the accused's mental state at the time of the offense rendered them incapable of forming the requisite criminal intent. For instance, if a defendant was suffering from a severe mental disorder that impaired their judgment and control over their actions, the court might accept this as a valid excuse. The determination of lack of capacity is highly fact-specific and requires thorough examination of the defendant's mental condition and the circumstances surrounding the alleged crime.

qa_pairs.answer: The purpose of a preliminary hearing in the criminal justice process is to determine whether there is sufficient reason to hold the accused for trial. During this hearing, the judge assesses the evidence presented by the prosecution to decide if there is enough basis to proceed with the case. If the judge finds that there is sufficient reason, the accused can be sent to jail or be permitted to make bail. Bail is a sum of money paid to the court to secure the defendant’s attendance at trial. If the accused fails to appear for the trial, they forfeit the bail money. qa_pairs.question: What happens after the defendant is indicted by a grand jury?
qa_pairs.answer: After the defendant is indicted by a grand jury, they formally become a defendant in the criminal justice process. The next step is the arraignment, where the defendant is brought before a judge to answer the charges outlined in the indictment. During the arraignment, the defendant has the option to plead guilty or not guilty. If the defendant pleads not guilty, the case will proceed to trial before a jury, also known as a petit jury. The jury's role is to determine the defendant's guilt or innocence based on the evidence presented during the trial. The jury must find the defendant guilty beyond a reasonable doubt to convict. Throughout the process, the defendant may also engage in plea bargaining with the prosecution, where they might plead guilty to the offense or a lesser charge in exchange for a more lenient sentence recommendation from the prosecutor. Additionally, the defendant has the option to file a plea of nolo contendere (no contest), which means they neither affirm nor deny their guilt, and they may be sentenced as though they had pleaded guilty.

The defendant is also permitted to file a plea of nolo contendere (no contest) in prosecutions for 
certain crimes. In so doing, he neither affirms nor denies his guilt. He may be sentenced as though he 
had pleaded guilty, although usually a nolo plea is the result of a plea bargain. Why plead nolo? In 
some offenses, such as violations of the antitrust laws, the statutes provide that private plaintiffs may 
use a conviction or a guilty plea as proof that the defendant violated the law. This enables a plaintiff 
to prove liability without putting on witnesses or evidence and reduces the civil trial to a hearing 
about the damages to plaintiff. The nolo plea permits the defendant to avoid this, so that any plaintiff 
will have to not only prove damages but also establish civil liability.

Following a guilty plea or a verdict of guilt, the judge will impose a sentence after presentencing 
reports are written by various court officials (often, probation officers). Permissible sentences are 
spelled out in statutes, though these frequently give the judge a range within which to work (e.g., 
twenty years to life). The judge may sentence the defendant to imprisonment, a fine, or both, or may 
decide to suspend sentence (i.e., the defendant will not have to serve the sentence as long as he stays 
out of trouble). 
 
Sentencing usually comes before appeal. As in civil cases, the defendant, now convicted, has the right 
to take at least one appeal to higher courts, where issues of procedure and constitutional rights may 
be argued. 
 
KEY TAKEAWAY 
 
Criminal procedure in US courts is designed to provide a fair process to both criminal defendants and to 
society. The grand jury system, prosecutorial discretion, plea bargains, and appeals for lack of a fair trial are all 
part of US criminal procedure.

qa_pairs.question: What is the purpose of a nolo contendere plea in criminal proceedings, and how does it benefit the defendant?
qa_pairs.answer: A nolo contendere plea, also known as a 'no contest' plea, is used by a defendant in certain criminal cases to avoid formally admitting guilt while still accepting the consequences of the plea. The primary purpose of this plea is to prevent the defendant from having a conviction used as an admission of guilt in subsequent civil litigation. For instance, in cases involving violations of antitrust laws, a conviction or guilty plea can be used as evidence of liability in a civil lawsuit. By pleading nolo contendere, the defendant avoids this potential use of their plea in civil proceedings, thereby protecting themselves from having their plea used against them in future civil cases. This plea is often the result of a plea bargain, where the defendant agrees to plead nolo contendere in exchange for a more favorable sentence or other concessions from the prosecution. While the defendant does not admit guilt, they may still be sentenced as though they had pleaded guilty, but the nolo plea can be strategically advantageous in avoiding certain legal complications in civil matters.

qa_pairs.question: What are the steps involved in the sentencing process following a guilty plea or verdict of guilt in US courts?
qa_pairs.answer: Following a guilty plea or verdict of guilt, the sentencing process in US courts involves several key steps. Initially, the judge will review presentencing reports, which are prepared by various court officials, often including probation officers. These reports provide detailed information about the defendant's background, criminal history, and other relevant factors that may influence the sentencing decision. The judge then considers the statutory guidelines, which outline permissible sentences for the specific crime committed. These guidelines typically provide a range within which the judge can exercise discretion, such as a range of twenty years to life for certain offenses. The judge has the authority to impose a sentence that includes imprisonment, a fine, or both, or may choose to suspend the sentence, meaning the defendant will not have to serve the full sentence as long as they do not commit further offenses. The sentencing process is designed to ensure that the punishment is proportionate to the crime and takes into account the individual circumstances of the defendant. Sentencing usually occurs before the defendant has the opportunity to appeal, although they retain the right to appeal the conviction itself on grounds of procedural errors or violations of constitutional rights.

6.6 Constitutional Rights of the Accused 
 
LEARNING OBJECTIVES 
 
1. Describe the most significant constitutional rights of defendants in US courts, and name the source of 
these rights. 
2. Explain the Exclusionary rule and the reason for its existence. 
 
 
Search and Seizure 
The rights of those accused of a crime are spelled out in four of the ten constitutional amendments that 
make up the Bill of Rights (Amendments Four, Five, Six, and Eight). For the most part, these 
amendments have been held to apply to both the federal and the state governments. The Fourth 
Amendment says in part that “the right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and 
effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated.” Although there are numerous 
and tricky exceptions to the general rule, ordinarily the police may not break into a person’s house or 
confiscate his papers or arrest him unless they have a warrant to do so. This means, for instance, that a 
policeman cannot simply stop you on a street corner and ask to see what is in your pockets (a power the 
police enjoy in many other countries), nor can your home be raided without probable cause to believe that 
you have committed a crime. What if the police do search or seize unreasonably? 
The courts have devised a remedy for the use at trial of the fruits of an unlawful search or seizure. 
Evidence that is unconstitutionally seized is excluded from the trial. This is the so-called exclusionary 
rule, first made applicable in federal cases in 1914 and brought home to the states in 1961. 
The exclusionary rule is highly controversial, and there are numerous exceptions to it. But it remains

qa_pairs.question: What is the Exclusionary rule and why was it established?
qa_pairs.answer: The Exclusionary rule is a legal principle in the United States that prevents evidence collected or analyzed in violation of the defendant's constitutional rights from being used in a court of law. This rule was established to deter law enforcement officers from conducting unlawful searches and seizures, thereby protecting the constitutional rights of individuals. The rule was first made applicable in federal cases in 1914 and was later extended to state courts in 1961. The Exclusionary rule is highly controversial, with numerous exceptions to it. However, its primary purpose remains to uphold the integrity of the judicial process by ensuring that evidence obtained through unconstitutional means is not used to convict individuals. This rule is rooted in the Fourth Amendment, which protects citizens from unreasonable searches and seizures, and is a fundamental aspect of the Bill of Rights.

qa_pairs.question: What are the constitutional rights of defendants in US courts, and what amendments protect these rights?
qa_pairs.answer: The constitutional rights of defendants in US courts are primarily outlined in the Bill of Rights, which comprises the first ten amendments to the United States Constitution. These rights are designed to protect individuals from abuses of power by the government and ensure a fair trial. The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures, requiring law enforcement to obtain a warrant based on probable cause before conducting a search or seizure. The Fifth Amendment guarantees the right to due process, protection against self-incrimination, and prohibits double jeopardy. The Sixth Amendment ensures the right to a speedy and public trial, an impartial jury, and the right to counsel. The Seventh Amendment preserves the right to a jury trial in civil cases. The Eighth Amendment prohibits excessive bail, excessive fines, and cruel and unusual punishment. The Ninth Amendment states that the enumeration of certain rights in the Constitution does not deny or disparage other rights retained by the people. The Tenth Amendment reserves powers not delegated to the federal government to the states or the people. These amendments collectively provide a robust framework for protecting the rights of defendants in the US judicial system.

The Sixth Amendment also says that the defendant shall have the right to confront witnesses against him. 
No testimony is permitted to be shown to the jury unless the person making it is present and subject to 
cross-examination by the defendant’s counsel. 
 
Assistance of Counsel 
The Sixth Amendment guarantees criminal defendants the right to have the assistance of defense counsel. 
During the eighteenth century and before, the British courts frequently refused to permit defendants to 
have lawyers in the courtroom during trial. The right to counsel is much broader in this country, as the 
result of Supreme Court decisions that require the state to pay for a lawyer for indigent defendants in 
most criminal cases. 
 
Cruel and Unusual Punishment 
Punishment under the common law was frequently horrifying. Death was a common punishment for 
relatively minor crimes. In many places throughout the world, punishments still persist that seem cruel 
and unusual, such as the practice of stoning someone to death. The guillotine, famously in use during and 
after the French Revolution, is no longer used, nor are defendants put in stocks for public display and 
humiliation. In pre-Revolutionary America, an unlucky defendant who found himself convicted could face 
brutal torture before death. 
 
The Eighth Amendment banned these actions with the words that “cruel and unusual punishments [shall 
not be] inflicted.” Virtually all such punishments either never were enacted or have been eliminated from 
the statute books in the United States. Nevertheless, the Eighth Amendment has become a source of 
controversy, first with the Supreme Court’s ruling in 1976 that the death penalty, as haphazardly applied 
in the various states, amounted to cruel and unusual punishment. Later Supreme Court opinions have 
made it easier for states to administer the death penalty. As of 2010, there were 3,300 defendants on 
death row in the United States. Of course, no corporation is on death row, and no corporation’s charter 
has ever been revoked by a US state, even though some corporations have repeatedly been indicted and 
convicted of criminal offenses.

qa_pairs.question: What is the purpose of the Speedy Trial Act enacted by Congress in 1975, and what is the standard time frame for criminal prosecutions to go to trial according to this law?
qa_pairs.answer: The Speedy Trial Act, enacted by Congress in 1975, was designed to give priority to criminal cases in federal courts by ensuring that all criminal prosecutions are brought to trial within a specified time frame. The standard time frame set by this law is seventy-five days. However, the law also lists many permissible reasons for delay, allowing for some flexibility in certain circumstances. The primary goal of the Speedy Trial Act is to prevent undue and prolonged pre-trial detention and to ensure that defendants receive a prompt resolution to their cases, thereby upholding the principles of justice and fairness.

qa_pairs.question: How has the right to counsel evolved in the United States, and what are the implications of Supreme Court decisions on the provision of legal representation for indigent defendants?
qa_pairs.answer: The right to counsel in the United States has undergone significant evolution, particularly influenced by Supreme Court decisions. During the eighteenth century and before, British courts often denied defendants the right to have lawyers present in the courtroom during their trials. In contrast, the right to counsel in the United States is much broader today. This expansion is largely due to Supreme Court rulings that mandate the state to provide legal representation for indigent defendants in most criminal cases. These decisions ensure that all defendants, regardless of their financial status, have access to competent legal defense, thereby promoting fairness and equality in the judicial process. The implications of these rulings are profound, as they help to prevent the disparity in legal representation that could otherwise lead to unjust outcomes for those who cannot afford private counsel. By guaranteeing the assistance of defense counsel, the Supreme Court has reinforced the fundamental principle that justice should be accessible to all individuals, not just those with financial means.

Presumption of Innocence 
The most important constitutional right in the US criminal justice system is the presumption of 
innocence. The Supreme Court has repeatedly cautioned lower courts in the United States that juries must 
be properly instructed that the defendant is innocent until proven guilty. This is the origin of the “beyond 
all reasonable doubt” standard of proof and is an instruction given to juries in each criminal case. The 
Fifth Amendment notes the right of “due process” in federal proceedings, and the Fourteenth Amendment 
requires that each state provide “due process” to defendants. 
 
KEY TAKEAWAY 
 
The US Constitution provides several important protections for criminal defendants, including a prohibition on 
the use of evidence that has been obtained by unconstitutional means. This would include evidence seized in 
violation of the Fourth Amendment and confessions obtained in violation of the Fifth Amendment.

qa_pairs.question: What was the main legal issue addressed in United States v. Dotterweich, and what was the Court's decision regarding the prosecution of corporations under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938?
qa_pairs.answer: The main legal issue addressed in United States v. The Court decided that both the corporation and its responsible individuals, such as managers, could be held liable under the Act. Instead, it placed the burden of acting at hazard upon individuals who were in responsible positions within the corporation. Therefore, individuals who share responsibility in the business process resulting in a violation of the Act are subject to its criminal provisions.

Summary 
Criminal law is that branch of law governing offenses against society. Most criminal law requires a specific 
intent to commit the prohibited act (although a very few economic acts, made criminal by modern 
legislation, dispense with the requirement of intent). In this way, criminal law differs from much of civil 
law—for example, from the tort of negligence, in which carelessness, rather than intent, can result in 
liability.

Major crimes are known as felonies. Minor crimes are known as misdemeanors. Most people have a 
general notion about familiar crimes, such as murder and theft. But conventional knowledge does not 
suffice for understanding technical distinctions among related crimes, such as larceny, robbery, and false 
pretenses. These distinctions can be important because an individual can be found guilty not merely for 
committing one of the acts defined in the criminal law but also for attempting or conspiring to commit 
such an act. It is usually easier to convict someone of attempt or conspiracy than to convict for the main 
crime, and a person involved in a conspiracy to commit a felony may find that very little is required to put 
him into serious trouble.

qa_pairs.question: What is the significance of intent in criminal law, and how does it differentiate criminal law from civil law?
qa_pairs.answer: Intent plays a crucial role in criminal law, distinguishing it from civil law. In criminal law, most offenses require a specific intent to commit the prohibited act. This means that for an individual to be found guilty of a crime, it must be proven that they had the conscious objective or purpose to engage in the criminal conduct. This requirement of intent ensures that only those who deliberately choose to break the law are held criminally liable. In contrast, civil law, such as the tort of negligence, does not always require intent. Instead, it can hold individuals liable for their actions if they were careless or negligent, even if they did not intend to cause harm. This distinction is important because it affects the burden of proof and the nature of the legal consequences. In criminal cases, the prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant had the requisite intent, which is a higher standard of proof compared to civil cases, where the standard is typically a preponderance of the evidence or clear and convincing evidence. Therefore, the requirement of intent in criminal law serves to differentiate it from civil law by focusing on the deliberate nature of the prohibited conduct.

qa_pairs.question: How can an individual be found guilty of attempting or conspiring to commit a crime, and why might it be easier to convict someone of these than of the main crime?
qa_pairs.answer: An individual can be found guilty of attempting or conspiring to commit a crime even if the main crime is not completed. Attempting a crime involves taking a substantial step towards committing the crime but failing to complete it. Conspiracy, on the other hand, involves an agreement between two or more people to commit a crime, along with some overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy. Convicting someone of attempting or conspiring to commit a crime can be easier than convicting them of the main crime because the prosecution does not need to prove that the crime was actually completed. Instead, they only need to demonstrate that the individual had the intent to commit the crime and took a significant step towards its completion or agreed to participate in the criminal plan. This lower threshold of proof can make it more feasible to secure a conviction, as it requires less evidence to show that the individual was involved in the criminal activity. Additionally, the mere fact that someone was involved in a conspiracy or attempted a crime can be sufficient for a conviction, even if the intended crime was not carried out. This aspect of criminal law serves as a deterrent, as individuals may be held accountable for their involvement in criminal plans, even if the plans are not fully realized.

qa_pairs.question: Does Tectonics have a double-jeopardy defense against the federal prosecution for bribery in Nigeria?
qa_pairs.answer: The concept of double jeopardy, which prevents an individual from being tried twice for the same offense, is a principle found in the Fifth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution. However, this protection applies within the jurisdiction of the United States. In the scenario described, Tectonics, a U.S. corporation, is involved in a bribery case in Nigeria. Since the alleged crime occurred outside the United States, the double jeopardy defense would not apply. Double jeopardy protects against being tried twice for the same crime within the same jurisdiction, but it does not extend to foreign jurisdictions. Therefore, Tectonics could potentially face prosecution in Nigeria for the bribery offense, and the U.S. corporation would not be shielded by the double jeopardy clause of the U.S. Constitution in this case.

qa_pairs.question: Can Ted Nelson and Jamie Skillset be found guilty of a crime related to the bribery of the Nigerian public official Adetutu Adeleke?
qa_pairs.answer: In the given scenario, Ted Nelson, the CEO of Tectonics, is not directly involved in the bribery of the Nigerian public official Adetutu Adeleke. However, Jamie Skillset, the CFO, is aware of the bribery and the securing of the contract by Whoopi Goldmine, a Nigerian employee of Tectonics. Under U.S. law, particularly the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA), it is illegal for U.S. companies and their employees to bribe foreign officials to obtain or retain business. The FCPA applies to all U.S. persons and certain foreign issuers of securities. It also applies to foreign firms and persons who take any act in furtherance of such a corrupt payment while in the United States. Given that Skillset is aware of the bribery and does not take steps to prevent it, both Nelson and Skillset could potentially be found guilty of a crime under the FCPA. Nelson, as the CEO, could be held responsible for the actions of the company and its employees, while Skillset could be held accountable for failing to report the bribery and for not taking appropriate action to stop it. The FCPA also includes provisions for corporate liability, which means that the company itself can be held liable for the actions of its employees. Therefore, Tectonics, as a corporation, could also face legal consequences for the bribery, and Nelson and Skillset could be individually prosecuted for their roles in the matter.

qa_pairs.question: What are the three kinds of torts mentioned in the text?
qa_pairs.answer: The three kinds of torts mentioned in the text are intentional torts, negligent torts, and strict liability torts. Intentional torts occur when a person intentionally causes harm to another, such as in cases of assault or battery. Negligent torts arise when a person fails to exercise reasonable care, leading to unintentional harm, such as in cases of negligence. Strict liability torts do not require proof of negligence or intent; instead, liability is imposed based on the nature of the activity or the product involved, regardless of fault.

qa_pairs.question: What is the purpose of damage awards in tort law according to the text?
qa_pairs.answer: The purpose of damage awards in tort law, as outlined in the text, is to adjust for harms done by awarding damages to a successful plaintiff who demonstrates that the defendant caused their losses. This legal remedy aims to compensate the injured party for their losses and restore them, as much as possible, to the position they were in before the tort occurred. The law seeks to provide a fair and just resolution by ensuring that the party responsible for the harm is held accountable and that the victim receives appropriate compensation for their injuries or damages.

Although the word is no longer in general use, tort suits are the stuff of everyday headlines. More and

The law of torts developed almost entirely in the common-law courts; that is, statutes passed by 
legislatures were not the source of law that plaintiffs usually relied on. Usually, plaintiffs would rely on the 
common law (judicial decisions). Through thousands of cases, the courts have fashioned a series of rules 
that govern the conduct of individuals in their noncontractual dealings with each other. Through 
contracts, individuals can craft their own rights and responsibilities toward each other. In the absence of 
contracts, tort law holds individuals legally accountable for the consequences of their actions. Those who 
suffer losses at the hands of others can be compensated. 
 
Many acts (like homicide) are both criminal and tortious. But torts and crimes are different, and the 
difference is worth noting. A crime is an act against the people as a whole. Society punishes the murderer; 
it does not usually compensate the family of the victim. Tort law, on the other hand, views the death as a 
private wrong for which damages are owed. In a civil case, the tort victim or his family, not the state,

qa_pairs.question: What is the primary difference between torts and crimes according to the text?
qa_pairs.answer: The primary difference between torts and crimes, as outlined in the text, lies in the nature of the wrong and the parties involved. A crime is considered an act against the people as a whole, and society punishes the perpetrator, typically through imprisonment or fines, without usually compensating the victim's family. In contrast, tort law views the harm as a private wrong for which damages are owed. In a civil case, the tort victim or their family, rather than the state, brings the action against the defendant. The judgment in a civil tort suit is usually expressed in monetary terms, aiming to compensate the victim for their loss rather than to punish the wrongdoer.

qa_pairs.question: Why do tort suits often make headlines, and what types of cases are commonly involved?
qa_pairs.answer: Tort suits often make headlines because they involve individuals seeking redress for wrongs that have caused them harm, and these cases can result in significant monetary awards. The text mentions that more people are injured by various risks and now seek remedies through the courts, leading to high-profile cases. Commonly involved cases include those against doctors who have bungled operations, newspapers that have libeled subjects of stories, and oil companies that have caused environmental devastation. These cases are examples of tort suits where the plaintiffs seek compensation for the losses they have suffered due to the actions of others.

Kinds of Torts 
There are three kinds of torts: intentional torts, negligent torts, and strict liability torts. Intentional torts 
arise from intentional acts, whereas unintentional torts often result from carelessness (e.g., when a 
surgical team fails to remove a clamp from a patient’s abdomen when the operation is finished). Both 
intentional torts and negligent torts imply some fault on the part of the defendant. In strict liability torts, 
by contrast, there may be no fault at all, but tort law will sometimes require a defendant to make up for 
the victim’s losses even where the defendant was not careless and did not intend to do harm. 
 
Dimensions of Tort Liability 
There is a clear moral basis for recovery through the legal system where the defendant has been careless 
(negligent) or has intentionally caused harm. Using the concepts that we are free and autonomous beings 
with basic rights, we can see that when others interfere with either our freedom or our autonomy, we will 
usually react negatively. As the old saying goes, “Your right to swing your arm ends at the tip of my nose.” 
The law takes this even one step further: under intentional tort law, if you frighten someone by swinging 
your arms toward the tip of her nose, you may have committed the tort of assault, even if there is no actual 
touching (battery). 
Under a capitalistic market system, rational economic rules also call for no negative externalities. That is, 
actions of individuals, either alone or in concert with others, should not negatively impact third parties. 
The law will try to compensate third parties who are harmed by your actions, even as it knows that a 
money judgment cannot actually mend a badly injured victim.

qa_pairs.question: What are the three kinds of torts and how do they differ in terms of the defendant's fault?
qa_pairs.answer: The three kinds of torts are intentional torts, negligent torts, and strict liability torts. Intentional torts arise from intentional acts by the defendant, implying that the defendant had a specific intent to cause harm or engage in wrongful conduct. Negligent torts, on the other hand, result from carelessness or failure to exercise reasonable care, indicating that the defendant did not intend to cause harm but was at fault due to negligence. Strict liability torts differ from the other two types as they do not require any fault on the part of the defendant. In strict liability cases, the defendant may not have been careless or intended to cause harm, but the law still holds them liable for the victim's losses. This means that even if the defendant took all necessary precautions and did not act negligently, they can still be held responsible for the harm caused.

qa_pairs.question: How does tort law address the concept of negative externalities in a capitalistic market system?
qa_pairs.answer: Tort law addresses the concept of negative externalities in a capitalistic market system by ensuring that actions of individuals or groups do not negatively impact third parties. In a capitalistic market, rational economic rules call for no negative externalities, meaning that the actions of individuals should not harm others. Tort law aims to compensate third parties who are harmed by the actions of others, even though a money judgment cannot fully mend the victim's injuries. By holding defendants liable for the harm caused to third parties, tort law seeks to internalize the costs of negative externalities and promote responsible behavior. This approach helps to maintain a fair and efficient market system by ensuring that individuals and entities are held accountable for the consequences of their actions on others.

Dimensions of Tort: Excuses 
A third element in the law of torts is the excuse for committing an apparent wrong. The law does not 
condemn every act that ultimately results in injury. 
 
One common rule of exculpation is assumption of risk. A baseball fan who sits along the third base line 
close to the infield assumes the risk that a line drive foul ball may fly toward him and strike him. He will 
not be permitted to complain in court that the batter should have been more careful or that management 
should have either warned him or put up a protective barrier. 
 
Another excuse is negligence of the plaintiff. If two drivers are careless and hit each other on the highway, 
some states will refuse to permit either to recover from the other. Still another excuse is consent: two 
boxers in the ring consent to being struck with fists (but not to being bitten on the ear).

qa_pairs.question: What are some of the protected interests that can be redressed in tort law, and can you provide examples of how mental suffering might be compensated?
qa_pairs.answer: Tort law protects various interests, including physical injury, mental suffering, reputation, privacy, and economic interests. For instance, mental suffering can be compensated if it results from a physical injury, such as shock and depression following an automobile accident. Some states even allow recovery for mental distress alone, as seen in cases where a mother experiences shock at seeing her son injured by a car while they were crossing the street. Other protected interests include a person's reputation, which can be injured by defamatory statements or writings, and privacy, which can be violated by the disclosure of personal secrets. Economic interests are also protected, with remedies available for misrepresentation to secure an economic advantage or certain forms of unfair competition.

qa_pairs.question: Under what circumstances might a court refuse to permit a plaintiff to recover damages in a tort case, and what are some examples of excuses that can be used to justify the defendant's actions?
qa_pairs.answer: A court might refuse to permit a plaintiff to recover damages in a tort case under several circumstances, including when the plaintiff has assumed the risk of injury, when the plaintiff's own negligence contributed to the harm, or when the plaintiff consented to the risk of harm. For example, a baseball fan who sits close to the infield assumes the risk of being struck by a foul ball and cannot claim damages. Similarly, if two drivers are careless and hit each other on the highway, some states will not allow either to recover from the other due to their own negligence. Consent is another excuse, as seen in boxing, where two boxers consent to being struck with fists but not to being bitten on the ear. These excuses serve to limit the liability of the defendant in situations where the plaintiff's own actions or decisions contributed to the harm or where the plaintiff voluntarily accepted the risk of harm.

Punitive damages are rarely allowed in negligence cases for that reason. But if someone sets out 
intentionally and maliciously to hurt another person, punitive damages may well be appropriate. Punitive 
damages are intended not only to punish the wrongdoer, by exacting an additional and sometimes heavy 
payment (the exact amount is left to the discretion of jury and judge), but also to deter others from similar 
conduct. The punitive damage award has been subject to heavy criticism in recent years in cases in which 
it has been awarded against manufacturers. One fear is that huge damage awards on behalf of a multitude 
of victims could swiftly bankrupt the defendant. Unlike compensatory damages, punitive damages are 
taxable.

There are three kinds of torts, and in two of them (negligent torts and strict liability torts), damages are 
usually limited to making the victim whole through an enforceable judgment for money damages. These 
compensatory damages awarded by a court accomplish only approximate justice for the injuries or property 
damage caused by a tortfeasor. Tort laws go a step further toward deterrence, beyond compensation to the

qa_pairs.question: What is the primary purpose of punitive damages in tort law, and in what situations are they typically awarded?
qa_pairs.answer: Punitive damages in tort law are primarily intended to punish the defendant for their actions and to deter similar conduct by others. They are typically awarded in situations where the defendant has deliberately committed a wrong with malicious intent or has engaged in behavior that is considered outrageous. These damages are not commonly awarded in negligence cases, as the general purpose of tort law is to compensate the victim rather than punish the wrongdoer. However, in cases of intentional torts, punitive damages may be appropriate to address the egregious nature of the defendant's actions. The exact amount of punitive damages is left to the discretion of the jury and the judge, and they are subject to heavy criticism, especially when awarded against manufacturers, due to concerns that large damage awards could bankrupt the defendant. Unlike compensatory damages, punitive damages are also taxable.

qa_pairs.question: Why are compensatory damages considered to provide only approximate justice for the injuries or property damage caused by a tortfeasor?
qa_pairs.answer: Compensatory damages are considered to provide only approximate justice for the injuries or property damage caused by a tortfeasor because they are designed to make the victim whole by covering the actual losses incurred. These damages are calculated based on the extent of the harm, such as medical expenses, lost wages, and property repair costs. However, compensatory damages may not fully account for the intangible aspects of harm, such as pain and suffering, emotional distress, or loss of enjoyment of life. As a result, the compensation provided may not fully reflect the true impact of the tortfeasor's actions on the victim's life. In contrast, punitive damages go beyond mere compensation by imposing costs on the wrongdoer to punish them and deter others from engaging in similar conduct. This additional layer of justice aims to address the moral and societal implications of the tortfeasor's actions, which compensatory damages alone may not fully capture.

LEARNING OBJECTIVES 
 
1. Distinguish intentional torts from other kinds of torts. 
2. Give three examples of an intentional tort—one that causes injury to a person, one that causes injury to 
property, and one that causes injury to a reputation. 
The analysis of most intentional torts is straightforward and parallels the substantive crimes already 
discussed in Chapter 6 "Criminal Law". When physical injury or damage to property is caused, there is 
rarely debate over liability if the plaintiff deliberately undertook to produce the harm. Certain other 
intentional torts are worth noting for their relevance to business. 
 
Assault and Battery 
One of the most obvious intentional torts is assault and battery. Both criminal law and tort law serve to 
restrain individuals from using physical force on others. Assault is (1) the threat of immediate harm or 
Saylor URL: http://www.saylor.org/books 
 
Saylor.org 
 
 
288 
offense of contact or (2) any act that would arouse reasonable apprehension of imminent harm. Battery is 
unauthorized and harmful or offensive physical contact with another person that causes injury. 
 
Often an assault results in battery, but not always. In Western Union Telegraph Co. v. Hill, for example, 
the defendant did not touch the plaintiff’s wife, but the case presented an issue of possible assault even 
without an actual battery; the defendant employee attempted to kiss a customer across the countertop, 
couldn't quite reach her, but nonetheless created actionable fear (or, as the court put it, “apprehension”) 
on the part of the plaintiff's wife. It is also possible to have a battery without an assault. For example, if 
someone hits you on the back of the head with an iron skillet and you didn’t see it coming, there is a 
battery but no assault. Likewise, if Andrea passes out from drinking too much at the fraternity party and a 
stranger (Andre) kisses her on the lips while she is passed out, she would not be aware of any threat of 
offensive contact and would have no apprehension of any harm. Thus there has been no tort of assault, 
but she could allege the tort of battery. (The question of what damages, if any, would be an interesting 
argument.)

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between assault and battery in the context of intentional torts?
qa_pairs.answer: Assault and battery are both intentional torts, but they differ in their elements and the type of harm they cause. Assault is defined as the threat of immediate harm or offensive contact, or any act that would arouse reasonable apprehension of imminent harm. It does not require physical contact; the mere threat or attempt to cause harm can constitute assault. Battery, on the other hand, involves unauthorized and harmful or offensive physical contact with another person that causes injury. Battery requires actual physical contact, whereas assault does not. For example, if someone raises a fist and threatens to hit another person, that would be considered assault. If the person then follows through and hits the other person, that would be considered battery. Both torts are intentional, meaning the perpetrator intended to cause harm or offensive contact.

qa_pairs.question: How does the doctrine of transferred intent apply to intentional torts, and can you provide an example?
qa_pairs.answer: The doctrine of transferred intent applies to intentional torts by transferring the intent from the intended victim to the actual victim. This means that if a person intends to commit a tort against one individual but accidentally harms another, the intent is transferred to the actual victim, and the perpetrator can still be held liable for the tort. For example, if Draco aims his wand at Harry but Harry ducks just in time and the impact is felt by Hermione instead, English law (and American law) would transfer Draco’s intent to Hermione. Draco would still be liable for the tort of battery against Hermione, even though he did not intend to harm her. The doctrine of transferred intent ensures that individuals are held accountable for their actions, even if the harm was not inflicted on the intended target.

Malicious Prosecution 
Malicious prosecution is the tort of causing someone to be prosecuted for a criminal act, knowing that 
there was no probable cause to believe that the plaintiff committed the crime. The plaintiff must show that 
the defendant acted with malice or with some purpose other than bringing the guilty to justice. A mere 
complaint to the authorities is insufficient to establish the tort, but any official proceeding will support the 
claim—for example, a warrant for the plaintiff’s arrest. The criminal proceeding must terminate in the 
plaintiff’s favor in order for his suit to be sustained. 
 
A majority of US courts, though by no means all, permit a suit for wrongful civil proceedings. Civil 
litigation is usually costly and burdensome, and one who forces another to defend himself against baseless 
accusations should not be permitted to saddle the one he sues with the costs of defense. However, 
because, as a matter of public policy, litigation is favored as the means by which legal rights can be 
vindicated—indeed, the Supreme Court has even ruled that individuals have a constitutional right to 
litigate—the plaintiff must meet a heavy burden in proving his case. The mere dismissal of the original 
lawsuit against the plaintiff is not sufficient proof that the suit was unwarranted. The plaintiff in a suit for 
wrongful civil proceedings must show that the defendant (who was the plaintiff in the original suit) filed 
the action for an improper purpose and had no reasonable belief that his cause was legally or factually 
well grounded. 
 
Defamation 
Defamation is injury to a person’s good name or reputation. In general, if the harm is done through the 
spoken word—one person to another, by telephone, by radio, or on television—it is called slander. If the 
defamatory statement is published in written form, it is called libel.

The Restatement (Second) of Torts defines a defamatory communication as one that “so tends to harm the 
reputation of another as to lower him in the estimation of the community or to deter third persons from 
associating or dealing with him.” [3] 
 
A statement is not defamatory unless it is false. Truth is an absolute defense to a charge of libel or slander. 
Moreover, the statement must be “published”—that is, communicated to a third person. You cannot be 
libeled by one who sends you a letter full of false accusations and scurrilous statements about you unless a 
third person opens it first (your roommate, perhaps). Any living person is capable of being defamed, but 
the dead are not. Corporations, partnerships, and other forms of associations can also be defamed, if the 
statements tend to injure their ability to do business or to garner contributions. 
 
The statement must have reference to a particular person, but he or she need not be identified by name. A 
statement that “the company president is a crook” is defamatory, as is a statement that “the major 
network weathermen are imposters.” The company president and the network weathermen could show 
that the words were aimed at them. But statements about large groups will not support an action for 
defamation (e.g., “all doctors are butchers” is not defamatory of any particular doctor). 
The law of defamation is largely built on strict liability. That a person did not intend to defame is 
ordinarily no excuse; a typographical error that converts a true statement into a false one in a newspaper, 
magazine, or corporate brochure can be sufficient to make out a case of libel. Even the exercise of due care 
is usually no excuse if the statement is in fact communicated. Repeating a libel is itself a libel; a libel 
cannot be justified by showing that you were quoting someone else. Though a plaintiff may be able to 
prove that a statement was defamatory, he is not necessarily entitled to an award of damages. That is 
because the law contains a number of privileges that excuse the defamation. 
 
Publishing false information about another business’s product constitutes the tort of slander of quality, or 
trade libel. In some states, this is known as the tort of product disparagement. It may be difficult to 
establish damages, however. A plaintiff must prove that actual damages proximately resulted from the 
slander of quality and must show the extent of the economic harm as well.

This definition emphasizes the impact of the communication on the individual's reputation and social interactions.
