What we commonly refer to as “securities” are essentially worthless pieces of paper. Their inherent 
value lies in the interest in property or an ongoing enterprise that they represent. This disparity between 
the tangible property—the stock certificate, for example—and the intangible interest it represents gives 
rise to several reasons for regulation. First, there is need for a mechanism to inform the buyer accurately 
what it is he is buying. Second, laws are necessary to prevent and provide remedies for deceptive and 
manipulative acts designed to defraud buyers and sellers. Third, the evolution of stock trading on a 
massive scale has led to the development of numerous types of specialists and professionals, in dealings 
with whom the public can be at a severe disadvantage, and so the law undertakes to ensure that they do 
not take unfair advantage of their customers. 
 
The Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 are two federal statutes that 
are vitally important, having virtually refashioned the law governing corporations during the past half 
century. In fact, it is not too much to say that although they deal with securities, they have become the 
general federal law of corporations. This body of federal law has assumed special importance in recent 
years as the states have engaged in a race to the bottom in attempting to compete with Delaware’s 
permissive corporation law (see Chapter 14 "Corporation: General Characteristics and Formation"). 
 
What Is a Security? 
Securities law questions are technical and complex and usually require professional counsel. For the 
nonlawyer, the critical question on which all else turns is whether the particular investment or document 
is a security. If it is, anyone attempting any transaction beyond the routine purchase or sale through a 
broker should consult legal counsel to avoid the various civil and criminal minefields that the law has 
strewn about. 
 
The definition of security, which is set forth in the Securities Act of 1933, is comprehensive, but it does 
not on its face answer all questions that financiers in a dynamic market can raise. Under Section 2(1) of 
the act, “security” includes “any note, stock, treasury stock, bond, debenture, evidence of indebtedness,

Under this definition, an investment may not be a security even though it is so labeled, and it may actually 
be a security even though it is called something else. For example, does a service contract that obligates

third party.” Under this test, courts have liberally interpreted “investment contract” and “certificate of 
interest or participation in any profit-sharing agreement” to be securities interests in such property as real 
estate condominiums and cooperatives, commodity option contracts, and farm animals. 
 
The Supreme Court ruled that notes that are not “investment contracts” under the Howey test can still be 
considered securities if certain factors are present, as discussed in Reves v. Ernst & Young, (see Section 
17.3.1 "What Is a Security?"). These factors include (1) the motivations prompting a reasonable seller and 
buyer to enter into the transaction, (2) the plan of distribution and whether the instruments are 
commonly traded for speculation or investment, (3) the reasonable expectations of the investing public, 
and (4) the presence of other factors that significantly reduce risk so as to render the application of the 
Securities Act unnecessary.

an offering or to bar the sale of securities if proper disclosures are made.

qa_pairs.answer: The SEC can refer the case to the Justice Department with a recommendation for criminal prosecution, seek a civil injunction in federal court against further violations, and proceed administratively by holding its own hearing before an administrative law judge. If the commissioners by majority vote accept the findings of the administrative law judge, they can impose a variety of sanctions, including suspending or expelling members of exchanges, denying, suspending, or revoking the registrations of broker-dealers, censuring individuals for misconduct, and barring censured individuals from employment with a registered firm. The 1990 securities law amendments also allow the SEC to impose civil fines similar to court-imposed fines and to order individuals to cease and desist from violating securities law.

qa_pairs.question: What is the fundamental mission of the SEC, and how does it relate to the Petrogene Oil & Gas Associates case?
qa_pairs.answer: The fundamental mission of the SEC is to ensure adequate disclosure in order to facilitate informed investment decisions by the public. The SEC does not have the authority to pass on the merits of an offering or to bar the sale of securities if proper disclosures are made. In the case of Petrogene Oil & Gas Associates, the SEC's regulatory mandate with respect to disclosures was highlighted when the company sold $274 million in limited partnership interests as a tax shelter. The company's filing with the SEC stated that the Petrogene offering was designed as a tax shelter, which was a significant disclosure that the SEC would have been responsible for ensuring was made to the public to facilitate informed investment decisions.

qa_pairs.question: What was the purpose of the Securities Act of 1933 and what are its primary objectives?
qa_pairs.answer: The Securities Act of 1933, also known as the 'truth in securities' law, was enacted to ensure full and fair disclosure of the character of securities sold in interstate and foreign commerce, as well as through the mails. Its primary objectives are to provide comprehensive information about the securities being offered and to prevent fraud in their sale. This is achieved through the requirement of registration, where issuers must file a registration statement and prospectus with the SEC, detailing relevant and material information about the offering. The SEC reviews these documents to ensure that all necessary disclosures are made, thereby protecting investors and maintaining the integrity of the securities market.

qa_pairs.question: What were some of the specific risks disclosed in the Petrogene Oil & Gas Associates offering, and why did the SEC permit the offering despite these risks?
qa_pairs.answer: The Petrogene Oil & Gas Associates offering disclosed several specific risks, including a high degree of risk, the potential for complete loss of investment, and the involvement of principals with criminal backgrounds and unregistered tax-sheltered securities. Additionally, the general partner had no experience in the company's proposed oil and gas operations, and one of the oils to be produced was potentially carcinogenic. Despite these alarming details, the SEC permitted the offering because all required disclosures were made. The SEC's role is to enforce securities laws and ensure that all material information is disclosed to investors, but it is ultimately the responsibility of the marketplace to determine whether the risks are worth taking. The SEC's decision to permit the offering was based on the premise that investors were provided with all the necessary information to make an informed decision about the investment.

qa_pairs.question: What must an issuer do before offering securities to the public under the Securities Act of 1933?
qa_pairs.answer: Before offering securities to the public under the Securities Act of 1933, an issuer must file a registration statement and prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). This registration statement and prospectus must provide detailed information about the offering, including relevant and material information about the issuer, the securities being offered, and the business and properties of the issuer. The SEC reviews the registration statement and prospectus to ensure they are not materially incomplete or inaccurate. If the SEC approves the registration statement, the issuer must then provide any prospective purchaser with the prospectus. The prospectus must contain all the information required by the SEC and cannot imply that the SEC has approved the securities for lack of merit. The registration statement and prospectus become public and are open for public inspection once filed, and the effective date of the registration statement is typically twenty days after filing. Until then, the offering cannot be made to the public.

qa_pairs.question: What are some exemptions from the registration requirement under the Securities Act of 1933?
qa_pairs.answer: Under the Securities Act of 1933, there are certain exemptions from the registration requirement for the sale of securities. One of the most important exemptions is Section 4(3), which exempts transactions by any person other than an issuer, such as brokers, dealers, and underwriters, from the registration requirement. Other exemptions include transactions by companies that are not required to register under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, private offerings to a limited number of sophisticated investors, and certain employee benefit plans. Additionally, there are exemptions for intrastate offerings, small offerings, and offerings of certain types of securities, such as government securities and municipal securities. These exemptions are designed to reduce the regulatory burden on smaller or less complex offerings while still protecting investors.

qa_pairs.question: What are the exemptions from the registration requirement under Section 4(3) of the Securities Act of 1933?
qa_pairs.answer: Section 4(3) of the Securities Act of 1933 provides several exemptions from the registration requirement for the sale of securities. One of the most significant exemptions is for transactions made by any person other than an issuer, underwriter, or dealer. This means that individuals or entities that are not involved in the issuance or underwriting of securities, or those who are not acting as dealers, are exempt from the need to register their securities transactions. Additionally, Section 4(3) exempts most transactions conducted by dealers, which includes brokers and dealers who facilitate the buying and selling of securities in the secondary market. As a result, trading in outstanding securities through brokers or dealers does not require a registration statement to be filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Other exemptions under Section 4(3) include private offerings to a limited number of persons or institutions who have access to the kind of information that registration would disclose and who do not intend to redistribute the securities. Offerings that are restricted to the residents of the state in which the issuing company is organized and doing business are also exempt. Furthermore, securities issued by municipal, state, federal, and other government instrumentalities, charitable institutions, banks, and carriers subject to the Interstate Commerce Act are exempt from registration. Offerings that do not exceed certain specified amounts and are made in compliance with SEC regulations are also exempt. Lastly, offerings of small business investment companies made in accordance with SEC rules and regulations are exempt from the registration requirement.

qa_pairs.question: What are the penalties for willful violations of the Securities Act of 1933?
qa_pairs.answer: The Securities Act of 1933 outlines specific penalties for willful violations of its provisions. Section 24 of the act stipulates that individuals who willfully make untrue statements of material fact or omit to state any material fact required to be stated in a registration statement, or necessary to make the statements therein not misleading, may face criminal penalties. These penalties include fines not exceeding $10,000 and a prison term not exceeding five years, or both. The term 'willful' in this context refers to actions taken with intent or reckless disregard for the truth. The act of making false declarations in registration statements, prospectuses, or oral communications concerning the sale of securities, as well as the unlawful failure of an issuer to register, are considered willful violations. Additionally, individuals who are injured by false declarations in connection with the sale of securities, or by the unlawful failure of an issuer to register, may file a civil suit to recover the net consideration paid for the security or for damages if the security has been sold. These civil penalty provisions apply specifically to false statements made in connection with the registration process and aim to protect investors from fraudulent activities and ensure the integrity of the securities market.

Securities Exchange Act of 1934 
Companies Covered 
The Securities Act of 1933 is limited, as we have just seen, to new securities issues—that is 
the primary market. The trading that takes place in the secondary market is far more significant, 
however. In a normal year, trading in outstanding stock totals some twenty times the value of new stock 
issues. 
 
To regulate the secondary market, Congress enacted the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. This law, 
which created the SEC, extended the disclosure rationale to securities listed and registered for public 
trading on the national securities exchanges. Amendments to the act have brought within its ambit every 
corporation whose equity securities are traded over the counter if the company has at least $10 million in 
assets and five hundred or more shareholders.

qa_pairs.question: What is the purpose of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and which companies does it cover?
qa_pairs.answer: The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 was enacted to regulate the secondary market, which is more significant than the primary market in terms of trading volume. The purpose of this act is to extend the disclosure rationale to securities that are listed and registered for public trading on national securities exchanges. It also created the SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission). The act covers every corporation whose equity securities are traded over the counter, provided the company has at least $10 million in assets and five hundred or more shareholders.

qa_pairs.question: What are the reporting requirements for companies under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934?

Penalties 
The logic of the Borak case (discussed in Section 17.1.3 "Securities Act of 1933") also applies to this act, so 
that private investors may bring suit in federal court for violations of the statute that led to financial 
injury. Violations of any provision and the making of false statements in any of the required disclosures 
subject the defendant to a maximum fine of $5 million and a maximum twenty-year prison sentence, but a 
defendant who can show that he had no knowledge of the particular rule he was convicted of violating 
may not be imprisoned. The maximum fine for a violation of the act by a person other than a natural 
person is $25 million. Any issuer omitting to file requisite documents and reports is liable to pay a fine of 
$100 for each day the failure continues. 
 
Blue Sky Laws 
Long before congressional enactment of the securities laws in the 1930s, the states had legislated 
securities regulations. Today, every state has enacted a blue sky law, so called because its purpose is to 
prevent “speculative schemes which have no more basis than so many feet of ‘blue sky.’” [3] The federal

Securities Act of 1933, discussed in Section 17.1.3 "Securities Act of 1933", specifically preserves the 
jurisdiction of states over securities. 
Blue sky laws are divided into three basic types of regulation. The simplest is that which prohibits fraud in 
the sale of securities. Thus at a minimum, issuers cannot mislead investors about the purpose of the 
investment. All blue sky laws have antifraud provisions; some have no other provisions. The second type 
calls for registration of broker-dealers, and the third type for registration of securities. Some state laws 
parallel the federal laws in intent and form of proceeding, so that they overlap; other blue sky laws 
empower state officials (unlike the SEC) to judge the merits of the offerings, often referred to as 
merit review laws. As part of a movement toward deregulation, several states have recently modified or 
eliminated merit provisions. 
 
Many of the blue sky laws are inconsistent with each other, making national uniformity difficult. In 1956, 
the National Conference of Commissioners on Uniform State Laws approved the Uniform Securities Act.

qa_pairs.question: What are the penalties for violations of the Securities Act of 1933, and under what conditions can a defendant avoid imprisonment?
qa_pairs.answer: Violations of the Securities Act of 1933 can result in severe penalties, including a maximum fine of $5 million and a maximum twenty-year prison sentence for individuals. However, a defendant can avoid imprisonment if they can demonstrate that they had no knowledge of the specific rule they were convicted of violating. For violations committed by entities other than natural persons, the maximum fine is increased to $25 million. Additionally, any issuer who fails to file the required documents and reports is subject to a fine of $100 for each day the failure continues. These penalties are designed to deter fraudulent activities and ensure that investors are protected from financial harm.

qa_pairs.question: How do blue sky laws differ from the Securities Act of 1933, and what are the three basic types of regulation under blue sky laws?
qa_pairs.answer: Blue sky laws, enacted by every state before the Securities Act of 1933, are designed to prevent speculative schemes and fraud in the sale of securities. These laws are preserved by the Securities Act of 1933, which allows states to continue regulating securities. Blue sky laws differ from the federal securities laws in that they are state-specific and can vary significantly from one state to another. The three basic types of regulation under blue sky laws are: 1) antifraud provisions, which prohibit issuers from misleading investors about the purpose of the investment; 2) registration of broker-dealers, which requires brokers to register with the state and adhere to certain standards; and 3) registration of securities, which mandates that securities be registered with the state before they can be sold. Some states also have merit review laws, which allow state officials to evaluate the merits of securities offerings. However, many blue sky laws are inconsistent with each other, making national uniformity challenging. In 1956, the National Conference of Commissioners on Uniform State Laws approved the Uniform Securities Act to promote consistency among state securities laws.

KEY TAKEAWAY 
 
The SEC administers securities laws to prevent the fraudulent practices in the sales of securities. The definition 
of security is intentionally broad to protect the public from fraudulent investments that otherwise would 
escape regulation. The Securities Act of 1933 focuses on the issuance of securities, and the Securities 
Exchange Act of 1934 deals predominantly with trading in issued securities. Numerous federal and state 
securities laws are continuously created to combat securities fraud, with penalties becoming increasingly 
severe.

The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act

qa_pairs.question: What is the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and what does it prevent American companies from doing?
qa_pairs.answer: The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) is a United States federal law that was enacted in 1977. Its primary purpose is to prevent American companies from engaging in bribery and other corrupt practices to gain business advantages in foreign countries. The FCPA prohibits U.S. companies and their employees from offering, paying, or promising to pay money or anything of value to foreign government officials, political parties, or candidates in order to influence their decisions or secure business advantages. This includes both direct bribes and indirect payments made through intermediaries. The FCPA also requires companies to maintain accurate books and records and to have a system of internal controls to prevent and detect bribery. Violations of the FCPA can result in severe penalties, including fines, imprisonment, and reputational damage. The Act applies to all U.S. persons and certain foreign issuers of securities, as well as foreign firms and persons who take any act in furtherance of such corrupt payment while in the United States.

qa_pairs.question: What are the key provisions of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and how has it amended the Securities Exchange Act of 1934?
qa_pairs.answer: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) was enacted in 2002 in response to a number of high-profile corporate scandals, including those involving Enron and WorldCom. The Act introduced significant changes to the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, with the aim of increasing corporate regulation, transparency, and accountability. Key provisions of SOX include the establishment of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) to oversee the audits of public companies, the requirement for CEOs and CFOs to certify the accuracy of financial statements, and the implementation of stricter penalties for fraudulent financial activity. SOX also introduced new requirements for internal controls and procedures to prevent fraud, as well as enhanced disclosure requirements for companies. The Act has significantly increased the responsibilities and liabilities of corporate executives, and has led to greater scrutiny of corporate governance practices. Overall, SOX has strengthened the regulatory framework for publicly traded companies, with the goal of protecting investors and restoring confidence in the financial markets.

The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act 
Investigations by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Watergate Special Prosecutor in 
the early 1970s turned up evidence that hundreds of companies had misused corporate funds, mainly by 
bribing foreign officials to induce them to enter into contracts with or grant licenses to US companies. 
Because revealing the bribes would normally be self-defeating and, in any event, could be expected to stir 
up immense criticism, companies paying bribes routinely hid the payments in various accounts. As a 
result, one of many statutes enacted in the aftermath of Watergate, the 
Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) of 1977, was incorporated into the 1934 Securities Exchange

falsity of the financial statements that are being filed. 
 
Congress’s response to abuses of financial reporting, the FCPA, was much broader than necessary to treat 
the violations that were uncovered. The FCPA prohibits an issuer (i.e., any US business enterprise), a 
stockholder acting on behalf of an issuer, and “any officer, director, employee, or agent” of an issuer from 
using either the mails or interstate commerce corruptly to offer, pay, or promise to pay anything of value 
to foreign officials, foreign political parties, or candidates if the purpose is to gain business by inducing 
the foreign official to influence an act of the government to render a decision favorable to the US 
corporation. 
 
But not all payments are illegal. Under 1988 amendments to the FCPA, payments may be made to

lawful under the written law of a foreign country. More important than the foreign-bribe provisions, the 
act includes accounting provisions, which broaden considerably the authority of the SEC. These 
provisions are discussed in SEC v. World-Wide Coin Investments, Ltd., [1] the first accounting provisions 
case brought to trial.

qa_pairs.question: What is the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) of 1977, and what are its main provisions?
qa_pairs.answer: The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) of 1977 is a United States law that was enacted in response to investigations by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Watergate Special Prosecutor, which revealed that many companies had misused corporate funds by bribing foreign officials to secure contracts or licenses. The FCPA was incorporated into the 1934 Securities Exchange Act to address these abuses. The main provisions of the FCPA prohibit an issuer (a US business enterprise), a stockholder acting on behalf of an issuer, and any officer, director, employee, or agent of an issuer from using the mails or interstate commerce corruptly to offer, pay, or promise to pay anything of value to foreign officials, foreign political parties, or candidates with the intent of gaining business by influencing the foreign official to render a decision favorable to the US corporation. However, the FCPA does allow for certain exceptions, such as payments made to expedite routine governmental actions, like obtaining a visa, and payments that are lawful under the written law of a foreign country. Additionally, the FCPA includes accounting provisions that significantly broaden the authority of the SEC, allowing for greater oversight and enforcement of financial reporting and corporate governance standards.

qa_pairs.question: How did the Sarbanes-Oxley Act amend the 1934 Securities Exchange Act, and what were the reasons for these amendments?
qa_pairs.answer: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act, enacted in 2002, amended the 1934 Securities Exchange Act to increase corporate regulation, transparency, and penalties for corporate misconduct. The amendments were a response to major corporate and accounting scandals, such as those involving Enron, Tyco International, and WorldCom, which shook investor confidence and highlighted significant weaknesses in corporate governance and financial reporting. Key provisions of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act include the establishment of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) to oversee the audits of public companies, the requirement for CEOs and CFOs to certify the accuracy of financial statements, and the implementation of stricter internal control requirements. The Act also increased penalties for fraudulent financial activity, enhanced the role of the SEC in enforcing securities laws, and introduced measures to protect whistleblowers. These amendments aimed to restore public trust in the financial markets by ensuring greater accountability and transparency in corporate financial practices.

Insider Trading 
Corporate insiders—directors, officers, or important shareholders—can have a substantial trading 
advantage if they are privy to important confidential information. Learning bad news (such as financial 
loss or cancellation of key contracts) in advance of all other stockholders will permit the privileged few to 
sell shares before the price falls. Conversely, discovering good news (a major oil find or unexpected 
profits) in advance gives the insider a decided incentive to purchase shares before the price rises. 
Because of the unfairness to those who are ignorant of inside information, federal law 
prohibits insider trading. Two provisions of the 1934 Securities Exchange Act are 
paramount: Section 16(b) and 10(b).

penalizes any such person by permitting the corporation or a shareholder suing on its behalf to recover

qa_pairs.question: What is the purpose of Section 16(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and how does it apply to corporate insiders?
qa_pairs.answer: Section 16(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 is designed to prevent corporate insiders, such as directors, officers, or shareholders owning 10 percent or more of a corporation's stock, from profiting from short-swing trading activities. This section penalizes insiders by allowing the corporation or a shareholder suing on its behalf to recover any profits made from buying and selling stock within a six-month period. The law applies to any company with more than $10 million in assets and at least five hundred or more shareholders of any class of stock. The purpose of Section 16(b) is to ensure fairness in the market by preventing insiders from using confidential information to their advantage, thereby protecting uninformed investors from unfair trading practices. For example, if an insider buys and sells stock within six months, they must return the profits made from these transactions to the corporation or its shareholders. This provision aims to deter insider trading and promote transparency and integrity in the financial markets.

qa_pairs.question: How does the SEC's authority under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) extend beyond the prohibition of foreign bribes, and what are the implications for companies?
qa_pairs.answer: The SEC's authority under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) extends beyond the prohibition of foreign bribes by including accounting provisions that significantly broaden the SEC's regulatory powers. These accounting provisions require companies to maintain accurate books and records and to devise and maintain an adequate system of internal accounting controls. The implications for companies are substantial, as they must ensure that their financial statements are free from falsification and that they have robust internal controls to prevent and detect improper payments or bribes. The SEC can bring enforcement actions against companies that fail to comply with these provisions, which can result in significant penalties, including fines and sanctions. The inclusion of accounting provisions in the FCPA underscores the SEC's commitment to promoting transparency and accountability in corporate financial practices, thereby protecting investors and maintaining the integrity of the financial markets.

qa_pairs.answer: Directors, officers, and large shareholders should avoid trading in their own company stock without legal advice due to the complexities and legal implications associated with insider trading. qa_pairs.answer: Rule 10b-5 is a regulation that prohibits any person from engaging in fraudulent or deceitful practices in connection with the purchase or sale of any security. It is not limited to securities registered under the 1934 Securities Exchange Act or publicly held companies; it applies to any security issued by any company, including the smallest closely held company. qa_pairs.question: What was the significance of the Texas Gulf Sulphur Company (TGS) case in relation to insider trading and Rule 10b-5?
qa_pairs.answer: The Texas Gulf Sulphur Company (TGS) case was significant in the context of insider trading and Rule 10b-5 as it marked the first major enforcement of the rule. In 1964, TGS discovered a rich deposit of copper and zinc, which led to a speculative frenzy in the Toronto Stock Exchange. The SEC charged several TGS officers and directors with purchasing or advising others to purchase TGS stock based on material inside information. The court ruled that the defendants who bought the stock before the public announcement had violated Rule 10b-5. This case established that anyone in possession of material inside information must either disclose it to the public or refrain from trading, setting a precedent for future insider trading cases.

qa_pairs.question: What is the significance of the Supreme Court's decision in Dirks v. Securities and Exchange Commission regarding tippee liability?
qa_pairs.answer: The Supreme Court's decision in Dirks v. Securities and Exchange Commission is significant because it established the principle that tippees (individuals who receive nonpublic information from insiders) are liable for insider trading if they knew or should have known that the insider breached a fiduciary duty by disclosing the information and if the insider received a personal benefit from the disclosure. This ruling clarified the conditions under which a tippee can be held responsible for insider trading, emphasizing the importance of the tippee's knowledge of the insider's breach of duty and the personal benefit received by the insider. The decision also reinforced the concept that insider trading laws are designed to protect the integrity of the securities markets by preventing unfair advantages gained through the misuse of confidential information.

qa_pairs.question: How does Rule 10b5-1, enacted by the SEC in 2000, affect the defense against insider trading allegations?
qa_pairs.answer: Rule 10b5-1, enacted by the SEC in 2000, significantly impacts the defense against insider trading allegations by defining trading 'on the basis of' inside information. According to this rule, a person is considered to be trading on the basis of inside information if they trade while aware of material nonpublic information. This means that even if a defendant claims that their trade was made independently of knowledge of the nonpublic information, they cannot use this argument as a defense under Rule 10b5-1. However, the rule also provides an affirmative defense for trades that were planned prior to the person receiving inside information. This means that if a person can demonstrate that their trade was planned before they became aware of the nonpublic information, they may be able to avoid liability for insider trading under this rule. Rule 10b5-1 thus creates a clear standard for determining when a trade is considered to be based on inside information, and it offers a potential defense for those who can prove pre-planned trading.

In 1987, in Carpenter v. United States, [8] the Supreme Court affirmed the conviction of a Wall Street 
Journal reporter who leaked advanced information about the contents of his “Heard on the Street” 
column. The reporter, who was sentenced to eighteen months in prison, had been convicted on both mail

Beyond these judge-made theories of liability, Congress had been concerned about insider trading, and in 
1984 and 1988, it substantially increased the penalties. A person convicted of insider trading now faces a 
maximum criminal fine of $1 million and a possible ten-year prison term. A civil penalty of up to three 
times the profit made (or loss avoided) by insider trading can also be imposed. This penalty is in addition 
to liability for profits made through insider trading. For example, financier Ivan Boesky, who was 
sentenced in 1987 to a three-year prison term for insider trading, was required to disgorge $50 million of 
profits and was liable for another $50 million as a civil penalty. In 2003, Martha Stewart was indicted on 
charges of insider trading but was convicted for obstruction of justice, serving only five months. More 
recently, in 2009, billionaire founder of the Galleon Group, Raj Rajaratnam, was arrested for insider 
trading; he was convicted in May 2011 of all 14 counts of insider trading. For the SEC release on the 
Martha Stewart case, seehttp://www.sec.gov/news/press/2003-69.htm. 
 
Companies that knowingly and recklessly fail to prevent insider trading by their employees are subject to 
a civil penalty of up to three times the profit gained or loss avoided by insider trading or $1 million, 
whichever is greater. Corporations are also subject to a criminal fine of up to $2.5 million.

Sarbanes-Oxley Act 
Congress enacted the Sarbanes-Oxley Act in 2002 in response to major corporate and accounting 
scandals, most notably those involving Enron, Tyco International, Adelphia, and WorldCom. The act 
created the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board, which oversees, inspects, and regulates 
accounting firms in their capacity as auditors of public companies. As a result of the act, the SEC may 
include civil penalties to a disgorgement fund for the benefit of victims of the violations of the Securities 
Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. 
 
KEY TAKEAWAY 
 
Corrupt practices, misuse of corporate funds, and insider trading unfairly benefit the minority and cost the 
public billions. Numerous federal laws have been enacted to create liability for these bad actors in order to 
prevent fraudulent trading activities. Both civil and criminal penalties are available to punish those actors who 
bribe officials or use inside information unlawfully.

qa_pairs.question: What are the four factors the court uses to determine whether or not the transaction involves a security?
qa_pairs.answer: The court uses four factors to determine whether a transaction involves a security. First, it examines the motivations behind the transaction, considering whether the seller aims to raise money for business purposes or to finance investments, and whether the buyer is interested in the profit the note is expected to generate. If the primary purpose is to raise money or finance investments, and the buyer is interested in profit, the instrument is likely a security. Second, the court looks at the 'plan of distribution' of the instrument to see if it is intended for common trading for speculation or investment. Third, the court considers the reasonable expectations of the investing public, recognizing that instruments may be deemed securities based on public expectations, even if an economic analysis might suggest otherwise. Finally, the court examines whether there is another regulatory scheme in place that significantly reduces the risk of the instrument, making the application of the Securities Acts unnecessary.

qa_pairs.question: How does the definition of security in this case differ from the definition in Securities & Exchange Commission v. W. J. Howey?
qa_pairs.answer: The definition of security in this case differs from the definition in Securities & Exchange Commission v. W. J. Howey in several ways. In the Howey case, the Supreme Court established a test for what constitutes an investment contract, which is a type of security. The test includes an investment of money in a common enterprise with a reasonable expectation of profits to be derived from the efforts of others. In contrast, the definition of security in this case is broader and more flexible. It does not strictly adhere to the Howey test but instead considers a variety of factors, including the motivations of the parties involved, the plan of distribution, the expectations of the investing public, and the presence of other regulatory schemes. This approach allows for a more nuanced analysis of whether an instrument should be classified as a security, taking into account the specific circumstances of each transaction.

qa_pairs.question: When does a tippee assume a fiduciary duty to shareholders of a corporation?
qa_pairs.answer: A tippee assumes a fiduciary duty to shareholders of a corporation when they receive material nonpublic information from an insider, and they know or should know that the insider has breached their fiduciary duty by disclosing the information. This duty arises from the tippee's knowledge of the insider's breach and their subsequent use or disclosure of the information. The Supreme Court in Dirks v. SEC clarified that a tippee's duty to abstain from trading or disclosing the information depends on whether the insider has breached a fiduciary duty and whether the tippee knows or should know of this breach. If the tippee is aware that the insider is disclosing the information for personal gain or as a gift, they may also be liable for insider trading. However, if the tippee's purpose is to expose fraud or wrongdoing, as in the case of Dirks, they may not be considered to have assumed a fiduciary duty to the shareholders.

qa_pairs.question: Did Dirks violate any insider trading laws?
qa_pairs.answer: In the case of Dirks v. SEC, Dirks did not violate any insider trading laws. Dirks was an accountant who received nonpublic information about a fraud committed by an insider at Equity Funding Corporation of America. He passed this information to a journalist, who then published an article exposing the fraud. Dirks did not trade on the information himself, nor did he receive any personal benefit from disclosing the information. The Supreme Court held that Dirks did not have a duty to abstain from using the inside information he obtained, as he was not a participant in the insider's breach of fiduciary duty. The Court concluded that Dirks' actions were motivated by a desire to expose the fraud, and therefore, he did not violate insider trading laws.

qa_pairs.question: How does this case refine Rule 10b-5?
qa_pairs.answer: The Basic Inc v. Levinson case refined Rule 10b-5 by clarifying the standard of materiality that applies to preliminary merger discussions. The Supreme Court held that statements made during preliminary merger discussions are material if there is a substantial likelihood that a reasonable shareholder would consider it important in deciding how to vote on a merger proposal. The Court also addressed the issue of reliance, stating that a presumption of reliance may be appropriate in certifying a class action, but each class member must still show direct reliance on the misleading statements. This case established that the materiality standard under Rule 10b-5 is not limited to statements that have a direct impact on the price of a security, but also includes statements that could influence a reasonable investor's decision-making process.

probability that the event will occur and the anticipated magnitude of the event in light of the totality of

17.4 Summary and Exercises 
 
Summary 
Beyond state corporation laws, federal statutes—most importantly, the Securities Act of 1933 and the 
Securities Exchange Act of 1934—regulate the issuance and trading of corporate securities. The federal 
definition of security is broad, encompassing most investments, even those called by other names. 
 
The law does not prohibit risky stock offerings; it bans only those lacking adequate disclosure of risks. The 
primary means for realizing this goal is the registration requirement: registration statements, 
prospectuses, and proxy solicitations must be filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). 
Penalties for violation of securities law include criminal fines and jail terms, and damages may be 
awarded in civil suits by both the SEC and private individuals injured by the violation of SEC rules. A 1977 
amendment to the 1934 act is the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, which prohibits an issuer from paying a 
bribe or making any other payment to foreign officials in order to gain business by inducing the foreign 
official to influence his government in favor of the US company. This law requires issuers to keep accurate 
sets of books reflecting the dispositions of their assets and to maintain internal accounting controls to 
ensure that transactions comport with management’s authorization. 
 
The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 presents special hazards to those trading in public stock on the basis 
of inside information. One provision requires the reimbursement to the company of any profits made 
from selling and buying stock during a six-month period by directors, officers, and shareholders owning 
10 percent or more of the company’s stock. Under Rule 10b-5, the SEC and private parties may sue

insiders who traded on information not available to the general public, thus gaining an advantage in 
either selling or buying the stock. Insiders include company employees.

qa_pairs.question: How does the court determine what is or is not material information, and how does this differ from its previous rulings?
qa_pairs.answer: The court determines what is considered material information by evaluating whether a reasonable investor would view the information as significantly altering the total mix of information available. Material information is typically defined as information that could influence an investor's decision to buy, sell, or hold a security. This determination is based on factors such as the significance of the information to the company's business, the magnitude of the information, and the context in which it is presented. In the case discussed, the court vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with the opinion, indicating a shift in how material information is assessed. This may differ from previous rulings where the criteria for materiality might have been applied differently, potentially leading to a different outcome in the case. The vacating of the judgment suggests that the court found the previous determination of materiality to be insufficient or incorrect, necessitating a reevaluation in light of the court's current understanding and interpretation of what constitutes material information.

qa_pairs.question: What is the fraud-on-the-market theory, and how does it relate to the court's decision in this case?
qa_pairs.answer: The fraud-on-the-market theory is a legal doctrine used in securities fraud cases, particularly under Rule 10b-5. It posits that the price of a company's stock in an efficient market reflects all publicly available information. Therefore, when a company makes a false or misleading statement, it defrauds all investors who rely on the integrity of the market price. In the context of the court's decision, the fraud-on-the-market theory likely played a crucial role in determining the materiality of the information in question. The court's decision to vacate the judgment and remand the case suggests that the previous court may not have adequately considered the implications of the fraud-on-the-market theory in its assessment of materiality. By remanding the case, the higher court is allowing for a reevaluation of the materiality of the information based on this theory, which could lead to a different outcome in the case.

This chapter begins with a discussion of the various ways a corporation can expand. We briefly 
consider successor liability—whether a successor corporation, such as a corporation that purchases 
all of the assets of another corporation, is liable for debts, lawsuits, and other liabilities of the 
purchased corporation. We then turn to appraisal rights, which are a shareholder’s right to dissent 
from a corporate expansion. Next, we look at several aspects, such as jurisdiction and taxation, of

18.1 Corporate Expansion 
 
LEARNING OBJECTIVE 
 
1. Understand the four methods of corporate expansion: purchase of assets other than in the regular course 
of business, merger, consolidation, and purchase of stock in another corporation. 
 
 
In popular usage, “merger” often is used to mean any type of expansion by which one corporation 
acquires part or all of another corporation. But in legal terms, merger is only one of four methods of 
achieving expansion other than by internal growth. 
 
Purchase of Assets 
One method of corporate expansion is the purchase of assets of another corporation. At the most basic 
level, ABC Corporation wishes to expand, and the assets of XYZ Corporation are attractive to ABC. So ABC 
purchases the assets of XYZ, resulting in the expansion of ABC. After the purchase, XYZ may remain in 
corporate form or may cease to exist, depending on how many of its assets were purchased by ABC.

qa_pairs.question: What are the four methods of corporate expansion other than internal growth?
qa_pairs.answer: The four methods of corporate expansion other than internal growth are the purchase of assets other than in the regular course of business, merger, consolidation, and purchase of stock in another corporation. These methods allow a corporation to expand its operations and increase its market presence without relying solely on its own internal growth.

qa_pairs.question: What happens to XYZ Corporation after ABC Corporation purchases its assets?
qa_pairs.answer: After ABC Corporation purchases the assets of XYZ Corporation, XYZ may either remain in corporate form or cease to exist, depending on how many of its assets were purchased by ABC. If ABC purchases all of XYZ's assets, XYZ may cease to exist as a separate legal entity. However, if ABC only purchases a portion of XYZ's assets, XYZ may continue to operate as a separate corporation, albeit with a reduced scope of operations.

A merger begins when two or more corporations negotiate an agreement outlining the specifics of a 
merger, such as which corporation survives and the identities of management personnel. There are two 
main types of merger: a cash merger and a noncash merger. In a cash merger, the shareholders of the 
disappearing corporation surrender their shares for cash. These shareholders retain no interest in the 
surviving corporation, having been bought out. This is often called a freeze-out merger, since the 
shareholders of the disappearing corporation are frozen out of an interest in the surviving corporation. 
 
In a noncash merger, the shareholders of the disappearing corporation retain an interest in the surviving 
corporation. The shareholders of the disappearing corporation trade their shares for shares in the 
surviving corporation; thus they retain an interest in the surviving corporation when they become 
shareholders of that surviving corporation. 
 
Unless the articles of incorporation state otherwise, majority approval of the merger by both boards of 
directors and both sets of shareholders is necessary (see Figure 18.2 "Merger"). The shareholder majority 
must be of the total shares eligible to vote, not merely of the total actually represented at the special 
meeting called for the purpose of determining whether to merge.

qa_pairs.question: What happens to the shareholders of the disappearing corporation in a cash merger?
qa_pairs.answer: In a cash merger, the shareholders of the disappearing corporation surrender their shares for cash. This means that they receive a monetary payout for their shares, but they retain no interest in the surviving corporation. Essentially, they are bought out and their ownership in the disappearing corporation is terminated. This type of merger is often referred to as a freeze-out merger because the shareholders of the disappearing corporation are effectively frozen out of any future interest in the surviving corporation.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between a merger and a consolidation?
qa_pairs.answer: A merger and a consolidation are similar processes where two or more corporations combine to form a new entity. However, there are key differences between the two. In a merger, the surviving corporation absorbs the disappearing corporation, and the shareholders of the disappearing corporation may or may not retain an interest in the surviving corporation, depending on whether it is a cash or noncash merger. On the other hand, in a consolidation, the companies merge to form a completely new corporation. The shareholders of the disappearing corporation do not retain an interest in the surviving corporation, as the resulting entity is a new corporation altogether. Both mergers and consolidations require approval by the boards and shareholders of the involved corporations, and the resulting entity becomes effective when the secretary of state issues a certificate of merger or incorporation.

Purchase of Stock 
Takeovers 
The fourth method of expanding, purchase of a company’s stock, is more complicated than the other 
methods. The takeover has become a popular method for gaining control because it does not require an 
affirmative vote by the target company’s board of directors. In a takeover, the acquiring company 
appeals directly to the target’s shareholders, offering either money or other securities, often at a premium 
over market value, in exchange for their shares. The acquiring company usually need not purchase 100 
percent of the shares. Indeed, if the shares are numerous and widely enough dispersed, control can be 
achieved by acquiring less than half the outstanding stock. In our example, if Flying Truckman has 
shareholders, BCT would make an offer directly to those shareholders to acquire their shares.

In the case of closely held corporations, it is possible for a company bent on takeover to negotiate with 
each stockholder individually, making a direct offer to purchase his or her shares. That is impossible in 
the case of large publicly held companies since it is impracticable and/or too expensive to reach each 
individual shareholder. To reach all shareholders, the acquiring company must make a tender offer, which 
is a public offer to purchase shares. In fact, the tender offer is not really an offer at all in the technical 
sense; the tender offer is an invitation to shareholders to sell their shares at a stipulated price. The 
tender offer might express the price in cash or in shares of the acquiring company. Ordinarily, the offeror 
will want to purchase only a controlling interest, so it will limit the tender to a specified number of shares 
and reserve the right not to purchase any above that number. It will also condition the tender offer on 
receiving a minimum number of shares so that it need buy none if stockholders do not offer a threshold 
number of shares for purchase.

qa_pairs.question: What is a tender offer in the context of corporate takeovers, and how does it differ from a direct offer to individual shareholders?
qa_pairs.answer: A tender offer in the context of corporate takeovers is a public invitation to shareholders to sell their shares at a specified price, typically expressed in cash or shares of the acquiring company. Unlike a direct offer, which is made individually to each stockholder and is impractical for large publicly held companies due to the impracticality and expense of reaching each shareholder, a tender offer is made to all shareholders collectively. The offeror usually aims to purchase a controlling interest and may limit the tender to a specified number of shares, reserving the right not to purchase any above that number. Additionally, the tender offer may be conditioned on receiving a minimum number of shares, meaning the acquiring company may not need to buy any shares if the threshold is not met. This method allows the acquiring company to reach a large number of shareholders efficiently and at scale.

qa_pairs.question: What is a leveraged buyout (LBO), and how is it typically financed in the context of corporate takeovers?
qa_pairs.answer: A leveraged buyout (LBO) is a type of corporate takeover where the purchase is financed primarily through debt. In the context of corporate takeovers, an LBO involves investors who are members of the target corporation acquiring a controlling interest in the company. The financing for an LBO typically involves using a significant amount of borrowed money to fund the purchase, with the assets of the target company often serving as collateral for the loans. This method allows the acquiring company to leverage its financial resources to make a substantial investment in another company without having to provide a large amount of cash upfront. The use of debt in an LBO can amplify the potential returns on investment, as the acquiring company aims to generate enough cash flow from the target company to service the debt and eventually pay off the loans. However, it also increases the financial risk, as the success of the LBO depends on the target company's ability to generate sufficient revenue and profits to meet its debt obligations.

Leveraged Buyouts 
A tender offer or other asset purchase can be financed as a leveraged buyout (LBO), a purchase 
financed by debt. A common type of LBO involves investors who are members of the target corporation 
and/or outsiders who wish to take over the target or retain a controlling interest. These purchasers use the 
assets of the target corporation, such as its real estate or a manufacturing plant, as security for a loan to 
purchase the target. The purchasers also use other types of debt, such as the issuance of bonds or a loan, 
to implement the LBO.

of its holdings in the target company. Even when a tender offer has not been made, the Williams Act

qa_pairs.answer: A leveraged buyout (LBO) is a type of acquisition where the purchase is primarily financed through debt. This debt is secured by the assets of the target corporation, such as real estate or manufacturing plants, as well as through other forms of debt like bonds or loans. qa_pairs.question: What are the requirements under the federal Williams Act for someone who acquires more than 5 percent ownership of a corporation?
qa_pairs.answer: Under the federal Williams Act, any person who acquires more than 5 percent ownership of a corporation is required to file a statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). This statement must include details about the source of funds to be used in making the purchase, the purpose of the purchase, and the extent of the acquirer's holdings in the target company. The Williams Act, which amended the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, aims to provide transparency and protect investors by ensuring that they are informed about significant changes in corporate ownership. The Act also requires that any person who acquires more than 5 percent ownership of a corporation must file a statement within ten days of the acquisition.

Short-Form Mergers 
If one company acquires 90 percent or more of the stock of another company, it can merge with the target 
company through the so-called short-form merger. Only the parent company’s board of directors need 
approve the merger; consent of the shareholders of either company is unnecessary. 
 
Appraisal Rights 
If a shareholder has the right to vote on a corporate plan to merge, consolidate, or sell all or substantially 
all of its assets, that shareholder has the right to dissent and invoke appraisal rights. Returning again to 
BCT, Bob and Carol, as shareholders, are anxious to acquire Flying Truckman, but Ted is not sure of the 
wisdom of doing that. Ted could invoke his appraisal rights to dissent from an expansion involving Flying 
Truckman. The law requires the shareholder to file with the corporation, before the vote, a notice of 
intention to demand the fair value of his shares. If the plan is approved and the shareholder does not vote 
in favor, the corporation must send a notice to the shareholder specifying procedures for obtaining 
payment, and the shareholder must demand payment within the time set in the notice, which cannot be 
less than thirty days. Fair value means the value of shares immediately before the effective date of the 
corporate action to which the shareholder has objected. Appreciation and depreciation in anticipation of 
the action are excluded, unless the exclusion is unfair. 
 
If the shareholder and the company cannot agree on the fair value, the shareholder must file a petition 
requesting a court to determine the fair value. The method of determining fair value depends on the 
circumstances. When there is a public market for stock traded on an exchange, fair value is usually the

qa_pairs.question: What is the purpose of a bidder to wait several years before merging with the target company unless the target’s board agrees in advance to the merger?
qa_pairs.answer: The purpose of a bidder to wait several years before merging with the target company unless the target’s board agrees in advance to the merger is to ensure that the merger is in the best interest of the target company and its shareholders. This waiting period allows the target company’s board to thoroughly evaluate the proposed merger and determine whether it is a good fit for the company. It also gives the target company’s shareholders time to consider the merger and make an informed decision. In many cases, the merger itself is the reason for the bid, and these laws are especially powerful in protecting the interests of the target company and its shareholders. The Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals upheld Wisconsin’s third-generation law in 1989, stating that it did not violate the Commerce Clause and was not preempted by the Williams Act. The Supreme Court decided not to review the decision.

qa_pairs.question: What are appraisal rights and how do they work if a shareholder has the right to vote on a corporate plan to merge, consolidate, or sell all or substantially all of its assets?
qa_pairs.answer: Appraisal rights are a legal mechanism that allows a shareholder to dissent from a corporate plan to merge, consolidate, or sell all or substantially all of its assets. If a shareholder has the right to vote on such a plan, they can invoke their appraisal rights to dissent from the plan. The law requires the shareholder to file a notice of intention to demand the fair value of their shares before the vote. If the plan is approved and the shareholder does not vote in favor, the corporation must send a notice to the shareholder specifying procedures for obtaining payment. The shareholder must then demand payment within the time set in the notice, which cannot be less than thirty days. Fair value is defined as the value of shares immediately before the effective date of the corporate action to which the shareholder has objected, excluding appreciation and depreciation in anticipation of the action unless the exclusion is unfair. If the shareholder and the company cannot agree on the fair value, the shareholder must file a petition requesting a court to determine the fair value. The method of determining fair value depends on the circumstances. When there is a public market for stock traded on an exchange, fair value is usually the price quoted on the exchange. In some circumstances, other factors, such as net asset value and investment value, may assume greater importance.

KEY TAKEAWAY 
 
There are four main methods of corporate expansion. The first involves the purchase of assets not in the 
ordinary course of business. Using this method, the purchase expands the corporation. The second and third 
methods, merger and consolidation, are very similar: two or more corporations combine. In a merger, one of 
the merging companies survives, and the other ceases to exist. In a consolidation, the merging corporations 
cease to exist when they combine to form a new corporation. The final method is a stock purchase, 
accomplished via a tender offer, takeover, or leveraged buyout. Federal and state regulations play a significant 
role in takeovers and tender offers, particularly the Williams Act. A shareholder who does not wish to 
participate in a stock sale may invoke his appraisal rights and demand cash compensation for his shares.

qa_pairs.question: What are the state-imposed conditions on the admission of foreign corporations?
qa_pairs.answer: State-imposed conditions on the admission of foreign corporations are regulations and requirements that a foreign corporation must meet to legally operate within a state. These conditions are designed to protect the state's residents and ensure that foreign corporations adhere to the same standards as domestic corporations. One common condition is the requirement for foreign corporations to obtain a certificate of authority from the state in which they wish to conduct business. This process typically involves submitting an application that includes details about the corporation's purpose, the nature of its business, and its compliance with the state's laws. Additionally, foreign corporations may be required to appoint a registered agent with a physical address within the state, who will be responsible for receiving legal documents on behalf of the corporation. Some states also impose fees for the certificate of authority and other related filings. Another condition is the requirement for foreign corporations to comply with state-specific regulations, such as obtaining necessary licenses and permits, adhering to local tax laws, and following state corporate governance standards. Failure to meet these conditions can result in penalties, fines, or even the revocation of the corporation's right to operate within the state. Furthermore, states may have specific rules regarding the types of business activities that foreign corporations can engage in, and they may restrict certain industries or require additional scrutiny for foreign entities. Overall, state-imposed conditions on the admission of foreign corporations are designed to ensure that these entities operate in a manner that is consistent with state laws and regulations, thereby protecting the interests of the state's residents and maintaining a fair business environment.

qa_pairs.question: What are the potential consequences for a foreign corporation that fails to comply with state-imposed conditions for admission?
qa_pairs.answer: A foreign corporation that fails to comply with state-imposed conditions for admission may face several potential consequences. Firstly, the corporation may be denied the right to conduct business within the state, effectively preventing it from operating and generating revenue from its intended market. This denial can have significant financial implications, as the corporation may have invested time and resources in preparing for entry into the state, only to be unable to proceed. Additionally, the corporation may be subject to penalties and fines imposed by the state for non-compliance. These penalties can vary depending on the nature and severity of the violation, but they may include monetary fines, interest on unpaid fees, and additional costs associated with legal proceedings. In some cases, the state may also revoke the corporation's certificate of authority, which would require the corporation to reapply for admission and potentially undergo a more rigorous review process. Furthermore, non-compliance can damage the corporation's reputation, making it more difficult to establish trust and credibility with potential partners, customers, and investors. It may also lead to legal disputes, as the corporation could face lawsuits from state authorities or other affected parties. Overall, failing to comply with state-imposed conditions for admission can have serious and far-reaching consequences for a foreign corporation, impacting its ability to operate, its financial standing, and its reputation in the market.

A foreign corporation is a company incorporated outside the state in which it is doing business. A 
Delaware corporation, operating in all states, is a foreign corporation in forty-nine of them. 
 
Conditions on Admission to Do Business 
States can impose on foreign corporations conditions on admission to do business if certain constitutional 
barriers are surmounted. One potential problem is the Privileges and Immunities Clause in Article IV, 
Section 2, of the Constitution, which provides that “citizens shall be entitled to all privileges and 
immunities of citizens in the several states.” The Supreme Court has interpreted this murky language to 
mean that states may not discriminate between their own citizens and those of other states. For example, 
the Court voided a tax New Hampshire imposed on out-of-state commuters on the grounds that “the tax 
falls exclusively on the incomes of nonresidents.” [1] However, corporations are uniformly held not to be

citizens for purposes of this clause, so the states may impose burdens on foreign corporations that they do 
not put upon companies incorporated under their laws. But these burdens may only be imposed on 
companies that conduct intrastate business, having some level of business transactions within that state. 
 
Other constitutional rights of the corporation or its members may also come into play when states attempt 
to license foreign corporations. Thus when Arkansas sought to revoke the license of a Missouri 
construction company to do business within the state, the Supreme Court held that the state had acted 
unconstitutionally (violating Article III, Section 2, of the US Constitution) in conditioning the license on a 
waiver of the right to remove a case from the state courts to the federal courts. [2]

Typical Requirements for Foreign Corporations 
Certain preconditions for doing business are common to most states. Foreign corporations are required to 
obtain from the secretary of state a certificate of authority to conduct business. The foreign corporation 
also must maintain a registered office with a registered agent who works there. The registered agent may 
be served with all legal process, demands, or notices required by law to be served on the corporation. 
Foreign corporations are generally granted every right and privilege enjoyed by domestic corporations. 
 
These requirements must be met whenever the corporation transacts business within the state. As 
mentioned previously, some activities do not fall within the definition of transacting business and may 
be carried on even if the foreign corporation has not obtained a certificate of authority. These include 
filing or defending a lawsuit, holding meetings of directors or shareholders, maintaining bank accounts, 
maintaining offices for the transfer of the company’s own securities, selling through independent 
contractors, soliciting orders through agents or employees (but only if the orders become binding 
contracts upon acceptance outside the state), creating or acquiring security interests in real or personal 
property, securing or collecting debts, transacting any business in interstate commerce, and “conducting 
an isolated transaction that is completed within 30 days and that is not one in the course of repeated 
transactions of a like nature” (Revised Model Business Corporation Act, Section 15.01).

contracts; and personal liability on contracts by officers and directors. In some states, contracts made by a

qa_pairs.question: What are the typical requirements for foreign corporations to conduct business in a state?
qa_pairs.answer: Foreign corporations must obtain a certificate of authority from the secretary of state to conduct business in a state. Additionally, they are required to maintain a registered office within the state and appoint a registered agent who works at that office. The registered agent is responsible for receiving all legal process, demands, or notices that must be served on the corporation. Foreign corporations are generally afforded the same rights and privileges as domestic corporations. These requirements must be fulfilled whenever the corporation engages in business activities within the state. However, certain activities do not fall under the definition of transacting business and can be carried out even without a certificate of authority. These activities include filing or defending lawsuits, holding meetings of directors or shareholders, maintaining bank accounts, maintaining offices for the transfer of the company’s own securities, selling through independent contractors, soliciting orders through agents or employees (provided the orders become binding contracts upon acceptance outside the state), creating or acquiring security interests in real or personal property, securing or collecting debts, transacting any business in interstate commerce, and conducting an isolated transaction that is completed within 30 days and is not part of repeated transactions of a similar nature (Revised Model Business Corporation Act, Section 15.01).

qa_pairs.question: What are the penalties for a foreign corporation failing to comply with a state's statute requiring a certificate of authority?
qa_pairs.answer: A foreign corporation that fails to comply with a state's statute requiring a certificate of authority may face several penalties. Firstly, the corporation may not sue in the state courts to enforce its rights until it obtains the necessary certificate of authority. However, it can still defend any lawsuits brought against it. The state attorney general has the authority to collect civil penalties, which vary from state to state. Other sanctions that may be imposed include fines and penalties on taxes owed, fines and imprisonment of corporate agents, directors, and officers, nullification of corporate contracts, and personal liability on contracts by officers and directors. In some states, contracts made by a corporation that has failed to qualify are considered void. These penalties underscore the importance of foreign corporations complying with state statutes to avoid legal and financial repercussions.

Jurisdiction over Foreign Corporations 
Whether corporations are subject to state court jurisdiction depends on the extent to which they are 
operating within the state. If the corporation is qualified to do business within the state and has a 
certificate of authority or license, then state courts have jurisdiction and process may be served on the 
corporation’s registered agent. If the corporation has failed to name an agent or is doing business without 
a certificate, the plaintiff may serve the secretary of state on the corporation’s behalf. 
 
Even if the corporation is not transacting enough business within the state to be required to qualify for a 
certificate or license, it may still be subject to suit in state courts under long-arm statutes. These laws 
permit state courts to exercise personal jurisdiction over a corporation that has sufficient contacts with 
the state. 
 
The major constitutional limitation on long-arm statutes is the Due Process Clause. The Supreme Court 
upheld the validity of long-arm statutes applied to corporations in International Shoe Co. v. 
Washington. [3] But the long-arm statute will only be constitutionally valid where there are minimum 
contacts—that is, for a state to exercise personal jurisdiction over a foreign corporation, the foreign 
corporation must have at least “minimum contacts” the state. That jurisdictional test is still applied many 
years after the International Shoe decision was handed down. [4] Since International Shoe, the 
nationalization of commerce has given way to the internationalization of commerce. This change has 
resulted in difficult jurisdictional questions that involve conflicting policy considerations. [5]

qa_pairs.question: What are the potential consequences for corporate agents, directors, and officers if a corporation fails to qualify and incurs taxes owed, fines, and imprisonment?
qa_pairs.answer: If a corporation fails to qualify and incurs taxes owed, fines, and imprisonment, the consequences can be severe for its corporate agents, directors, and officers. They may face personal liability on contracts made by the corporation, meaning they could be held personally responsible for fulfilling the terms of those contracts. Additionally, they could be subject to nullification of corporate contracts, which would invalidate agreements made by the corporation. In some states, contracts made by a corporation that has failed to qualify are considered void, further complicating the legal standing of such agreements. This situation underscores the importance of ensuring that a corporation is properly qualified and licensed to operate within a state to avoid these significant legal and financial repercussions.

qa_pairs.question: Under what conditions can state courts exercise personal jurisdiction over foreign corporations according to long-arm statutes?
qa_pairs.answer: State courts can exercise personal jurisdiction over foreign corporations under long-arm statutes when the foreign corporation has sufficient contacts with the state. The Supreme Court's decision in International Shoe Co. v. Washington established that for a long-arm statute to be constitutionally valid, there must be 'minimum contacts' between the foreign corporation and the state. This means that the foreign corporation must have engaged in activities that are substantial enough to warrant the state's jurisdiction. These activities could include conducting business, owning property, or entering into contracts within the state. The Due Process Clause of the Constitution limits the application of long-arm statutes, ensuring that the exercise of jurisdiction is fair and reasonable. Since the International Shoe decision, the rise of international commerce has led to complex jurisdictional questions, balancing the need for states to regulate businesses within their borders with the principles of fair play and substantial justice.

question might seem surprising. Why should a state ever be barred from taxing foreign corporations 
licensed to do business in the state? If the foreign corporation was engaged in purely local, intrastate 
business, no quarrel would arise. The constitutional difficulty is whether the tax constitutes an 
unreasonable burden on the company’s interstate business, in violation of the Commerce Clause. The 
basic approach, illustrated in D. H. Holmes Co., Ltd. v. McNamara (see Section 18.4.2 "Constitutional 
Issues Surrounding Taxation of a Foreign Corporation"), is that a state can impose a tax on activities for 
which the state gives legal protection, so long as the tax does not unreasonably burden interstate 
commerce. 
 
State taxation of corporate income raises special concerns. In the absence of ground rules, a company 
doing business in many states could be liable for paying income tax to several different states on the basis 
of its total earnings. A company doing business in all fifty states, for example, would pay five times its 
earnings in income taxes if each state were to charge a 10 percent tax on those earnings. Obviously, such a 
result would seriously burden interstate commerce. The courts have long held, therefore, that the states 
may only tax that portion of the company’s earnings attributable to the business carried on in the state. To 
compute the proportion of a company’s total earnings subject to tax within the state, most states have 
adopted a formula based on the local percentage of the company’s total sales, property, and payroll. 
 
KEY TAKEAWAY 
 
A foreign corporation is a company incorporated outside of the state in which it is doing business. States can 
place reasonable limitations upon foreign corporations subject to constitutional requirements. A foreign 
corporation must do something that is sufficient to rise to the level of transacting business within a state in 
order to fall under the jurisdiction of that state. These transactions must meet the minimum-contacts 
requirement for jurisdiction under long-arm statutes. A state may tax a foreign corporation as long as it does 
not burden interstate commerce.
