qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between a real defense and a personal defense in the context of a holder in due course (HDC)?
qa_pairs.answer: In the context of a holder in due course (HDC), the distinction between real defenses and personal defenses is crucial. Real defenses are valid against any holder, including an HDC, and can be asserted to prevent the enforcement of the instrument. These defenses are considered universally applicable and include infancy, duress, fraud in the execution, forgery, and discharge in bankruptcy. On the other hand, personal defenses are specific to the parties involved in the transaction and cannot be used against an HDC. These defenses are typically related to the underlying contract or agreement and include fraud in the inducement, failure of consideration, nonperformance of a condition precedent, and similar issues. An HDC, who has acquired the instrument in good faith, for value, and without notice of any defects, is protected from personal defenses but not from real defenses. This means that while an HDC can enforce the instrument free from personal defenses raised by prior parties, they can still be challenged if a real defense is presented.

qa_pairs.question: How does the shelter rule apply to a person who could not have become an HDC directly?
qa_pairs.answer: The shelter rule allows a person who could not have become a holder in due course (HDC) directly to acquire the rights of an HDC by taking the instrument as a transferee from an HDC. This rule is based on the principle that the rights of an HDC should be preserved and passed on to subsequent holders. To benefit from the shelter rule, the transferee must not have been a party to any fraud or illegality affecting the instrument and must not have had notice of any defense or claim against the instrument at the time of the transfer. Essentially, the shelter rule provides a form of 'inheritance' of HDC status, allowing the transferee to step into the shoes of the original HDC and enjoy the protections and privileges that come with HDC status, such as immunity from personal defenses and the ability to enforce the instrument against all parties.

LEARNING OBJECTIVES 
 
1. Recognize what a signature is under Article 3 of the Uniform Commercial Code. 
2. Understand how a person’s signature on an instrument affects liability if the person is an agent, or a 
purported agent, for another. 
 
 
The liability of an agent who signs commercial paper is one of the most frequently litigated issues in this 
area of law. For example, Igor is an agent (treasurer) of Frank N. Stein, Inc. Igor signs a note showing that 
the corporation has borrowed $50,000 from First Bank. The company later becomes bankrupt. The 
question: Is Igor personally liable on the note? The unhappy treasurer might be sued by the bank—the 
immediate party with whom he dealt—or by a third party to whom the note was transferred (see Figure 
22.1 "Signature by Representative").

There are two possibilities regarding an agent who signs commercial paper: the agent was authorized to 
do so, or the agent was not authorized to do so. First, though, what is a signature? 
 
A “Signature” under the Uniform Commercial Code 
Section 3-401 of the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) provides fairly straightforwardly that “a signature 
can be made (i) manually or by means of a device or machine, and (ii) by the use of any name, including 
any trade or assumed name, or by any word, mark, or symbol executed or adopted by a person with the 
present intention to authenticate a writing.” 
 
Liability of an Agent Who Has Authority to Sign 
Agents often sign instruments on behalf of their principals, and—of course—because a corporation’s 
existence is a legal fiction (you can’t go up and shake hands with General Motors), corporations can only 
act through their agents.

qa_pairs.question: What is the liability of an agent who signs commercial paper on behalf of a principal under the Uniform Commercial Code?
qa_pairs.answer: Under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), an agent who signs commercial paper on behalf of a principal can be held personally liable if they were authorized to do so. The UCC defines a signature as any manual or device-based mark, name, or symbol executed with the intention to authenticate a writing. When an agent, such as a treasurer, signs a note indicating that a corporation has borrowed money, the corporation's liability is tied to the agent's authority. If the agent was authorized to sign the note, the principal (the corporation) is liable for the debt. However, if the agent was not authorized to sign, the principal may not be held liable, and the agent could be personally responsible for the debt. This distinction is crucial in determining the extent of liability and the potential for litigation against the agent or the principal.

qa_pairs.question: How does the Uniform Commercial Code define a signature, and what implications does this have for an agent signing on behalf of a corporation?
qa_pairs.answer: The Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) Section 3-401 defines a signature as any manual or device-based mark, name, or symbol executed with the intention to authenticate a writing. This broad definition includes signatures made by an agent on behalf of a corporation. For an agent signing on behalf of a corporation, this means that the signature is legally binding and authenticates the document. If the agent signs a negotiable instrument, such as a note or check, the corporation is bound by the terms of that instrument. The implications are significant: if the agent signs with authority, the corporation is liable for the obligations of the instrument. Conversely, if the agent signs without authority, the corporation may not be liable, and the agent could face personal liability. This underscores the importance of clear authorization and understanding of the agent's role and the legal effects of their signature.

Section 3-402(a) of the UCC provides that a person acting (or purporting to act) as an agent who signs an 
instrument binds the principal to the same extent that the principal would be bound if the signature were 
on a simple contract. The drafters of the UCC here punt to the common law of agency: if, under agency

makes clear he is doing so as an agent. In our example, Igor should sign as follows: “Frank N. Stein, Inc.,

Incorrect Signatures 
The problems arise where the agent, although authorized, signs in an incorrect way. There are three 
possibilities: (1) the agent signs only his own name—“Igor”; (2) the agent signs both names but without 
indication of any agency—“Frank N. Stein, Inc., / Igor” (the signature is ambiguous—are both parties to be 
liable, or is Igor merely an agent?); (3) the agent signs as agent but doesn’t identify the principal—“Igor, 
Agent.” 
 
The UCC provides that in each case, the agent is liable to a holder in due course (HDC) who took the 
instrument without notice that the agent wasn’t intended to be liable on the instrument. As to any other

instrument did not intend her to be liable on it. Section 3-402(c) says that, as to a check, if an agent signs 
his name without indicating agency status but the check has the principal’s identification on it (that would 
be in the upper left corner), the authorized agent is not liable.

qa_pairs.question: What is the liability of an agent who signs an instrument on behalf of a principal under Section 3-402(a) of the UCC?
qa_pairs.answer: Under Section 3-402(a) of the UCC, an agent who signs an instrument on behalf of a principal binds the principal to the same extent that the principal would be bound if the signature were on a simple contract. This means that if the principal would be liable for the instrument under common law agency principles, the agent's signature is considered the authorized signature of the principal. Therefore, the principal is held liable for the obligations of the instrument, and the agent is not personally liable, provided that the agent has the authority to sign on behalf of the principal.

qa_pairs.question: What are the consequences for an agent who signs an instrument in an incorrect manner according to the UCC?
qa_pairs.answer: If an agent signs an instrument incorrectly, the UCC outlines specific consequences depending on the nature of the incorrect signature. If the agent signs only his own name without indicating agency, he is liable to a holder in due course (HDC) who took the instrument without notice of the agent's lack of authority. The agent is also liable to any other person unless he can prove that the original parties did not intend him to be liable. If the agent signs both names but without indicating agency, the signature is ambiguous, and the agent may be held liable unless it can be shown that the original parties did not intend him to be liable. If the agent signs as an agent but does not identify the principal, he is liable to an HDC and to any other person unless he can prove the original parties did not intend him to be liable. However, if an agent signs his name without indicating agency status but the check has the principal's identification on it, the agent is not liable.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE 
 
1. Understand that a person who signs commercial paper incurs contract liability. 
2. Recognize the two types of such liability: primary and secondary. 
3. Know the conditions that must be met before secondary liability attaches. 
 
 
Two types of liability can attach to those who deal in commercial paper: contract liability and warranty 
liability. Contract liability is based on a party’s signature on the paper. For contract liability purposes, 
signing parties are divided into two categories: primary parties and secondary parties. 
 
We discuss here the liability of various parties. You may recall the discussion in Chapter 19 "Nature and 
Form of Commercial Paper" about accommodation parties. An accommodation party signs a negotiable 
instrument in order to lend his name to another party to the instrument. The Uniform Commercial Code 
(UCC) provides that such a person “may sign the instrument as maker, drawer, acceptor, or indorser” and 
that in whatever capacity the person signs, he will be liable in that capacity. [1]

qa_pairs.question: What is the liability of a person who signs a promissory note as a maker under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC)?
qa_pairs.answer: Under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), a person who signs a promissory note as a maker incurs contract liability. This means that the maker promises to pay the instrument according to the terms specified in the note. The obligation to pay is unconditional and is owed to the person entitled to enforce the note or to an indorser who has paid the note. The primary purpose of a promissory note is to create a binding promise to pay a specified amount of money, either on demand or at a future date, to a specified payee. The maker's liability is based on their signature on the note, making them directly responsible for fulfilling the payment obligation. This liability is distinct from warranty liability, which arises from the transfer of the note and involves different parties and conditions.

qa_pairs.question: Under what circumstances is a forgery effective as to the person whose name is forged according to the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC)?
qa_pairs.answer: According to the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), a forgery is generally ineffective as to the person whose name is forged. However, there are specific circumstances under which a forgery can be effective as to the forger. If the principal or the person paying on the instrument has been negligent in contributing to, or in failing to notice, the forgery, then comparative negligence principles are applied. This means that if the forgery is discovered and the negligence of the principal or the person paying on the instrument is established, the liability may be shared between the parties involved. The UCC aims to protect the integrity of commercial transactions by holding parties accountable for their actions and ensuring that forgery does not go unnoticed. In cases where negligence is proven, the UCC provides a framework for determining the extent of liability and the distribution of responsibility among the parties.

qa_pairs.question: What is the primary liability of the drawee when they sign a draft, and what happens if they accept the draft with variations in terms?
qa_pairs.answer: The primary liability of the drawee when they sign a draft is to honor the draft as presented. This means that the drawee, upon signing the draft, agrees to pay the amount specified in the draft to the holder or indorser. If the drawee accepts the draft with variations in terms, they become liable according to those varied terms. This acceptance must be written on the draft, and it can be accompanied by wording such as 'accepted,' 'good,' or 'I accept.' When a bank certifies a check, it acts as the drawee and becomes liable to the holder for payment. In such cases, the holder can look only to the bank, not to the drawer, for payment. The acceptance of the draft with variations in terms means that the drawee is agreeing to the new terms, and they will be responsible for fulfilling those terms if the draft is presented for payment.

qa_pairs.question: Under the revised UCC, what is the drawer's liability when a check they wrote is dishonored, and what was the requirement under the pre-1997 UCC?
qa_pairs.answer: Under the revised UCC, the drawer's liability when a check they wrote is dishonored is not conditioned upon notice of dishonor. This means that the drawer is still liable to pay the amount of the check according to its terms when they wrote it, or according to its terms when it was completed, subject to some limitations. This change simplifies the process for the holder, as they do not need to provide notice of dishonor to hold the drawer liable. Under the pre-1997 UCC, the drawer's liability was conditioned not only upon the dishonor of the check but also upon the provision of notice of dishonor to the drawer. This notice had to be given to the drawer for them to be held liable for the dishonored check. The requirement of notice of dishonor added an additional step for the holder to take before the drawer could be held responsible for the payment.

qa_pairs.question: What are the conditions that must be met for a drawer's liability to arise under the UCC for an unaccepted draft?
qa_pairs.answer: Under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), for a drawer's liability to arise for an unaccepted draft, two specific conditions must be met. First, the draft must be presented for payment, which means that the person entitled to enforce the instrument (typically the creditor) must demand payment from the maker or drawee of the draft. Second, the draft must be dishonored, meaning that the maker or drawee refuses to pay or accept the draft when it is presented. These conditions ensure that the drawer's liability is contingent upon the draft being presented and subsequently dishonored, thereby providing a clear framework for when the drawer can be held responsible for the payment.

qa_pairs.question: What is the significance of 'without recourse' indorsement for an indorser under the UCC?
qa_pairs.answer: The 'without recourse' indorsement is significant for an indorser under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) because it allows the indorser to disclaim contractual liability on the instrument. When an indorser adds 'without recourse' to their indorsement, they are essentially stating that they do not guarantee payment of the instrument. This means that if the instrument is dishonored, the indorser is not obligated to pay the amount due. The UCC recognizes this indorsement as a way for an indorser to limit their liability, and it is a common practice used to protect the indorser from potential financial loss if the instrument is not paid by the maker or acceptor.

qa_pairs.question: What is the civil equivalent of theft in the context of instruments according to the UCC?
qa_pairs.answer: The civil equivalent of theft in the context of instruments according to the UCC is conversion. Conversion occurs when an instrument is presented for payment or acceptance and the person to whom it is presented refuses to pay, accept, or return it. Additionally, an instrument is considered converted if a person pays it on a forged indorsement, such as when a bank pays a check on a forged indorsement, making the bank liable to the person whose indorsement was forged.

qa_pairs.question: Under what circumstances can a person enforce an obligation despite the theft of their check?
qa_pairs.answer: A person can enforce an obligation despite the theft of their check if the check was never delivered to the intended recipient, and the person who stole the check forged the indorsement to another party. For example, if A indorses a check to B and puts it in an envelope that is never delivered to B, and then Thief steals the envelope, forges B's indorsement, and obtains payment, A, as the original owner of the check, has a cause of action for conversion against Thief. B, who never obtained rights in the check, cannot enforce the obligation against A. However, B can still enforce the obligation against A, as A intended to negotiate the check to B in payment of an obligation, and the obligation was not affected by Thief's conduct.

qa_pairs.question: What is the UCC's stance on the form of notice required for dishonor of an instrument, and what are the implications for the parties involved?
qa_pairs.answer: The Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) stipulates that notice of dishonor does not need to adhere to a specific form; it is considered sufficient if it reasonably identifies the instrument and indicates that it has been dishonored or has not been paid or accepted. This notice can be given orally, in writing, or electronically, and it must be delivered in a commercially reasonable manner. The implications of this are significant for the parties involved. For instance, if a party presents an instrument for payment and it is dishonored, they must promptly notify any party who may be liable on the instrument. Failure to provide such notice can result in the party being discharged from liability. This means that if a party does not give notice of dishonor, they may lose their right to seek recourse from other parties who are liable on the instrument. The UCC also outlines specific time limits for giving notice of dishonor, which vary depending on whether the party is a collecting bank or another person. For example, an oral notice is generally unwise because it might be difficult to prove, and written notice is usually preferred. The UCC's approach to notice of dishonor aims to ensure that all parties are promptly informed of the dishonor, allowing them to take appropriate action to mitigate their losses.

qa_pairs.question: In the scenario where Ann refuses to pay Earl, who presented the note, what are the consequences for the secondary parties involved, and how does the order of indorsements affect their liability?
qa_pairs.answer: In the given scenario, Ann, the maker of the note, refuses to pay Earl, who presented the note. As a result, Earl must give notice of dishonor to the secondary parties, which are the indorsers in this case. The order of indorsements is crucial because it determines the sequence in which the secondary parties are liable. Earl must notify Darlene, the last indorser, before he can proceed against the others. If Earl only notifies Darlene, he can collect from her, but not from Betty or Carl. If Darlene wishes to be reimbursed, she must notify Betty and Carl. If she fails to notify either, she cannot seek recourse from them. If she notifies both, she may recover from either. Carl, in turn, may collect from Betty, as she was notified before Carl's indorsement. If Darlene notifies only Carl, she can only collect from him, and he must notify Betty to be reimbursed. If Earl only notifies Betty, Carl and Darlene are discharged from liability because they were not notified. The UCC's rules on notice of dishonor and the order of indorsements ensure that each party is aware of their potential liability and the need to notify others to preserve their rights to recourse.

There are some deadlines for giving notice: on an instrument taken for collection, a bank must give notice 
before midnight on the next banking day following the day on which it receives notice of dishonor; a 
nonbank must give notice within thirty days after the day it received notice; and in all other situations, the 
deadline is thirty days after the day dishonor occurred. [12] 
 
Waived or Excused Conditions 
Presentment and notice of dishonor have been discussed as conditions precedent for imposing liability 
upon secondarily liable parties (again, drawers and indorsers). But the UCC provides circumstances in 
which such conditions may be waived or excused. 
 
Presentment Waived or Excused 
Under UCC Section 3-504(a), presentment is excused if (1) the creditor cannot with reasonable diligence 
present the instrument; (2) the maker or acceptor has repudiated the obligation to pay, is dead, or is in 
insolvency proceedings; (3) no presentment is necessary by the instrument’s terms; (4) the drawer or 
indorsers waived presentment; (5) the drawer instructed the drawee not to pay or accept; or (6) the 
drawee was not obligated to the drawer to pay the draft. 
 
Notice of Dishonor Excused 
Notice of dishonor is not required if (1) the instrument’s terms do not require it or (2) the debtor waived 
the notice of dishonor. Moreover, a waiver of presentment is also a waiver of notice of dishonor. Delay in 
giving the notice is excused, too, if it is caused by circumstances beyond the control of the person giving 
notice and she exercised reasonable diligence when the cause of delay stopped. [13]

qa_pairs.question: What happens if Earl only notifies Betty about the dishonor of an instrument, and why can't he proceed against Carl and Darlene?
qa_pairs.answer: If Earl only notifies Betty about the dishonor of an instrument, he cannot proceed against Carl and Darlene because he did not notify them. According to the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), Earl must notify all parties who are secondarily liable on the instrument, including Carl and Darlene, to hold them liable. Betty, having indorsed the instrument subsequent to Earl, is not contractually obligated to him, and thus cannot proceed against Carl and Darlene. However, if Betty mistakenly believes she can collect from Carl or Darlene and gives them notice within the time allowed to Earl, Earl would be entitled to collect from one of them if Betty fails to pay, because they would have received notice. This is because notice operates for the benefit of all parties who have rights against the obligor, as stated in Section 3-503(b) of the UCC.

qa_pairs.question: Under what circumstances can presentment and notice of dishonor be waived or excused according to the UCC?
qa_pairs.answer: Presentment and notice of dishonor can be waived or excused under several circumstances as outlined by the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC). Presentment is excused if the creditor cannot with reasonable diligence present the instrument, the maker or acceptor has repudiated the obligation to pay, is dead, or is in insolvency proceedings, no presentment is necessary by the instrument’s terms, the drawer or indorsers waived presentment, the drawer instructed the drawee not to pay or accept, or the drawee was not obligated to the drawer to pay the draft. Notice of dishonor is excused if the instrument’s terms do not require it, the debtor waived the notice of dishonor, or a waiver of presentment is also a waiver of notice of dishonor. Additionally, delay in giving the notice is excused if it is caused by circumstances beyond the control of the person giving notice and they exercised reasonable diligence when the cause of delay stopped. These provisions ensure that the requirements for presentment and notice of dishonor are flexible and can be adapted to the specific circumstances of each case.

qa_pairs.question: What is the significance of presentment and notice of dishonor in the context of notes, according to the UCC?
qa_pairs.answer: Presentment and notice of dishonor are conditions that can affect the liability of parties involved in the negotiation of a note. According to the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), presentment is the demand made on the person obligated to pay the note, which can be the maker, acceptor, or drawee. Notice of dishonor is the communication to the parties liable on the note, such as endorsers, that the note has not been paid when due. These actions are significant because they can establish the rights and obligations of the parties involved. For instance, if presentment and notice of dishonor are not properly executed, it may affect the ability of the holder to recover the amount due from endorsers. However, the UCC acknowledges that in practice, these formalities are often waived, especially for notes like those for mortgages, student loans, or consumer debts. In such cases, the holder may not require formal presentment or notice of dishonor, as the expectation is that the debtor will make payments directly to the holder without the need for such formalities. This waiver of presentment and notice of dishonor simplifies the process for debtors and reduces the administrative burden on holders, while still allowing for the enforcement of the note's terms.

qa_pairs.question: Under what circumstances can delay in giving notice of dishonor be excused according to the UCC?
qa_pairs.answer: The Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) provides that delay in giving notice of dishonor can be excused if the delay is caused by circumstances beyond the control of the person giving the notice and if they have exercised reasonable diligence when the cause of delay stopped. This means that if unforeseen events occur that prevent the timely delivery of notice, such as natural disasters, accidents, or other emergencies, the person responsible for giving the notice may not be held liable for the delay. However, it is crucial that the person giving the notice demonstrates that they took reasonable steps to mitigate the delay as soon as the cause of it ceased. For example, if a person is unable to deliver the notice due to a sudden illness, they would need to show that they attempted to arrange for someone else to deliver the notice or that they communicated with the relevant parties as soon as they were able. The UCC's provision for excusing delay in notice of dishonor is designed to ensure fairness and to account for the unpredictable nature of certain events that can impede the timely communication of dishonor.

qa_pairs.question: What is the primary liability on a negotiable instrument and who are the parties involved?
qa_pairs.answer: The primary liability on a negotiable instrument is unconditional and is held by the makers of notes and drawees of drafts, such as banks for checks. This means that these parties are obligated to pay the instrument when it is presented for payment, regardless of any other conditions. The primary liability is a direct result of the contract that these parties enter into when they sign the negotiable instrument, agreeing to honor it. This liability is not dependent on the instrument being presented for payment or dishonored, although these actions can trigger secondary liability.

qa_pairs.question: What are the conditions precedent to secondary liability on a negotiable instrument?
qa_pairs.answer: Secondary liability on a negotiable instrument arises under specific conditions. Firstly, the instrument must have been presented for payment or collection by the primarily liable party, such as the maker of a note or the drawee of a draft. Secondly, the instrument must have been dishonored, meaning it was not paid when presented. Lastly, notice of dishonor must be provided to the secondarily liable parties, such as drawers and indorsers. These conditions ensure that secondary parties are only held liable when the primarily liable parties fail to fulfill their obligations. It's important to note that the presentment and notice of dishonor are often unnecessary to enforce contractual liability, but they are required to trigger secondary liability.

LEARNING OBJECTIVES 
 
1. Understand that independent of contract liability, parties to negotiable instruments incur warranty liability. 
2. Know what warranties a person makes when she transfers an instrument. 
3. Know what warranties a person makes when he presents an instrument for payment or acceptance. 
4. Understand what happens if a bank pays or accepts a check by mistake. 
 
 
Overview of Warranty Liability 
We discussed the contract liability of primary and secondary parties, which applies to those who sign the 
instrument. Liability arises a second way, too—by warranty. A negotiable instrument is a type of property 
that is sold and bought, just the way an automobile is, or a toaster. If you buy a car, you generally expect 
that it will, more or less, work the way cars are supposed to work—that’s the implied warranty of 
merchantability. Similarly, when an instrument is transferred from A to B for consideration, the 
transferee (B) expects that the instrument will work the way such instruments are supposed to work. If A 
transfers to B a promissory note made by Maker, B figures that when the time is right, she can go to 
Maker and get paid on the note. So A makes some implied warranties to B—transfer warranties. And 
when B presents the instrument to Maker for payment, Maker assumes that B as the indorsee from A is 
entitled to payment, that the signatures are genuine, and the like. So B makes some implied warranties to 
Maker—presentment warranties. Usually, claims of breach of warranty arise in cases involving forged, 
altered, or stolen instruments, and they serve to allocate the loss to the person in the best position to have 
avoided the loss, putting it on the person (or bank) who dealt with the wrongdoer. We take up both 
transfer and presentment warranties.

qa_pairs.question: What are transfer warranties and why are they important in the context of negotiable instruments?
qa_pairs.answer: Transfer warranties are a set of implied warranties that a person makes when transferring a negotiable instrument, such as a promissory note, to another party for consideration. These warranties are crucial because they ensure that the transferee (the person receiving the instrument) can rely on the instrument's validity and enforceability. When A transfers a promissory note made by Maker to B, A makes certain implied warranties to B, including the warranty that the instrument is genuine, that all signatures are authentic, and that there are no alterations or forgeries. These warranties are important because they provide a level of protection to the transferee, ensuring that the instrument will work as expected, just like other instruments are supposed to work. If the instrument turns out to be forged, altered, or stolen, the person in the best position to have avoided the loss, typically the person who dealt with the wrongdoer, is held responsible. This allocation of loss helps maintain trust and reliability in the transfer of negotiable instruments, which are often sold and bought like other types of property, such as automobiles or toasters.

qa_pairs.question: What happens if a bank pays or accepts a check by mistake, and what warranties are involved in this scenario?
qa_pairs.answer: If a bank pays or accepts a check by mistake, it may be held liable for the mistake. This situation involves presentment warranties, which are a set of implied warranties that a person makes when presenting a negotiable instrument, such as a check, for payment or acceptance. When B presents the instrument to Maker for payment, B makes certain implied warranties to Maker, including the warranty that B is entitled to payment, that the signatures on the instrument are genuine, and that there are no alterations or forgeries. If the bank pays or accepts the check by mistake, it may be held liable for breaching these warranties. The bank's liability arises because it assumed that B, as the indorsee from A, was entitled to payment and that the signatures were genuine. In such cases, the loss is allocated to the person or bank in the best position to have avoided the loss, typically the person who dealt with the wrongdoer. This allocation of loss helps maintain trust and reliability in the transfer and presentation of negotiable instruments, ensuring that the person in the best position to have avoided the loss is held responsible.

qa_pairs.question: What are the five implied warranties made by a person who receives consideration for transferring an instrument according to UCC Section 3-416?
qa_pairs.answer: The five implied warranties made by a person who receives consideration for transferring an instrument, as outlined in UCC Section 3-416, are as follows: 1. The transferor is entitled to enforce the instrument, meaning the transferor warrants that they are—or would have been if they weren’t transferring it—entitled to enforce the instrument. This warranty ensures that there are no unauthorized or missing indorsements that prevent the transferor from making the transferee a person entitled to enforce the instrument. 2. All signatures on the instrument are authentic and authorized, ensuring that the instrument has not been forged or tampered with. 3. The instrument has not been altered in any way, maintaining its original terms and conditions. 4. The instrument is not subject to any defense or claim in recoupment that can be asserted against the warrantor, meaning the transferee does not take on any undisclosed defenses or claims that could affect their right to enforce the instrument. 5. The transferee warrants that they are taking the instrument in good faith, which means they have no knowledge of any issues that could affect the instrument's enforceability.

qa_pairs.question: Under what circumstances can a transferee-holder sue a prior party on one or more of the five implied warranties according to UCC Section 3-416?
qa_pairs.answer: A transferee-holder can sue a prior party on one or more of the five implied warranties under UCC Section 3-416 in several circumstances. Firstly, if the transferor was not entitled to enforce the instrument at the time of transfer, the transferee-holder can sue the prior party for breach of the warranty that the transferor was entitled to enforce the instrument. Secondly, if there are unauthorized or missing indorsements that prevent the transferor from making the transferee a person entitled to enforce the instrument, the transferee-holder can sue the prior party for breach of the warranty regarding the authenticity and authorization of signatures. Thirdly, if the instrument has been altered in any way, the transferee-holder can sue the prior party for breach of the warranty that the instrument has not been altered. Fourthly, if the instrument is subject to a defense or claim in recoupment that can be asserted against the warrantor, the transferee-holder can sue the prior party for breach of the warranty that the instrument is not subject to such defenses or claims. Lastly, if the transfer was made in bad faith, the transferee-holder can sue the prior party for breach of the warranty that the transferee took the instrument in good faith. In all these cases, the transferee-holder can sue the prior party to recover damages or other remedies as provided by UCC Section 3-416.

qa_pairs.question: What happens if a bank pays a check with a forged drawer's signature, and the presenter of the check was unaware of the forgery?
qa_pairs.answer: If a bank pays a check with a forged drawer's signature and the presenter of the check was unaware of the forgery, the bank bears the loss. This is because the bank is responsible for verifying the authenticity of the drawer's signature before making a payment. The presenter, who presented the check to the bank, only warrants that they are entitled to enforce the instrument or obtain payment on it. If the presenter is not entitled to payment due to the forgery, the bank can hold the presenter liable for breach of warranty. However, the bank cannot charge the drawer's account because it did not follow the drawer's order in paying to the wrong person. The bank can, though, go back to the presenter for the amount paid. This rule applies to all cases where the presenter makes a warranty to the drawee paying out on an unaccepted draft, such as when a person cashes a check made out to them at the drawer's bank.

If the presenter is not entitled to payment, for example, because the drawer's signature was forged, the presenter can be held liable for breach of warranty. The presenter is responsible for the amount paid, and the bank can go back to the presenter for the amount paid. This rule applies to all cases where the presenter makes a warranty to the drawee paying out on an unaccepted draft, such as when a person cashes a check made out to them at the drawer's bank.

22.4 Discharge 
 
LEARNING OBJECTIVE 
 
1. Understand how the obligations represented by commercial paper may be discharged. 
 
 
Overview 
Negotiable instruments eventually die. The obligations they represent are discharged (terminated) in two 
general ways: (1) according to the rules stated in Section 3-601 of the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) or 
(2) by an act or agreement that would discharge an obligation to pay money under a simple contract (e.g., 
declaring bankruptcy). 
 
Discharge under the Uniform Commercial Code 
The UCC provides a number of ways by which an obligor on an instrument is discharged from liability, 
but notwithstanding these several ways, under Section 3-601, no discharge of any party provided by the 
Saylor URL: http://www.saylor.org/books 
 
Saylor.org 
 
 
908 
rules presented in this section operates against a subsequent holder in due course unless she has notice 
when she takes the instrument. 
 
Discharge in General 
Discharge by Payment 
A person primarily liable discharges her liability on an instrument to the extent of payment by paying or 
otherwise satisfying the holder, and the discharge is good even if the payor knows that another has claim 
to the instrument. However, discharge does not operate if the payment is made in bad faith to one who 
unlawfully obtained the instrument (and UCC Section 3-602(b) lists two other exceptions). 
 
 
 
Discharge by Tender 
A person who tenders full payment to a holder on or after the date due discharges any subsequent liability 
to pay interest, costs, and attorneys’ fees (but not liability for the face amount of the instrument). If the 
holder refuses to accept the tender, any party who would have had a right of recourse against the party 
making the tender is discharged. Mario makes a note payable to Carol, who indorses it to Ed. On the date 
the payment is due, Mario (the maker) tenders payment to Ed, who refuses to accept the payment; he 
would rather collect from Carol. Carol is discharged: had she been forced to pay as indorser in the event of 
Mario’s refusal, she could have looked to him for recourse. Since Mario did tender, Ed can no longer look 
to Carol for payment. [1] 
 
Discharge by Cancellation and Renunciation

qa_pairs.question: What are the two general ways by which an obligor on an instrument is discharged from liability according to the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC)?
qa_pairs.answer: An obligor on an instrument is discharged from liability in two general ways according to the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC). The first way is by following the rules stated in Section 3-601 of the UCC, which outlines specific conditions under which an obligor can be discharged from their obligations. The second way is through an act or agreement that would discharge an obligation to pay money under a simple contract, such as declaring bankruptcy. These methods ensure that the obligations represented by commercial paper are eventually terminated, either through legal provisions or through mutual agreements between the parties involved.

qa_pairs.question: How does tender of full payment to a holder on or after the date due discharge a person from subsequent liability on an instrument?
qa_pairs.answer: Tender of full payment to a holder on or after the date due discharges a person from subsequent liability on an instrument by satisfying the holder's claim. This means that the person who made the tender, in this case Mario, is no longer obligated to pay interest, costs, and attorneys' fees related to the instrument. However, it does not discharge the person from liability for the face amount of the instrument. If the holder refuses to accept the tender, any party who would have had a right of recourse against the person making the tender is also discharged. For example, if Mario tendered payment to Ed, who refused to accept it, Ed would no longer be able to look to Carol, the indorser, for payment. This discharge is effective even if Mario knew that another party had a claim to the instrument, provided the payment was made in good faith.

Impairment of Collateral 
If the obligor’s duty to pay is secured by an interest in collateral and the holder impairs the value of the 
interest in collateral, the obligation of an indorser or accommodation party having a right of recourse 
against the obligor is discharged to the extent of the impairment.

party also become liable to pay the note (by signing it as a co-maker or by indorsing the note). In 
suretyship law, the accommodation party is a “Surety.” Then Bank agrees to a modification of the 
rights and obligations between it and Principal Debtor, such as agreeing that she may pay the 
note at some date after the due date, or that she may discharge her $10,000 obligation to pay the

is discharged if changes like this are made by Bank (the creditor) without Surety’s consent to the 
extent Surety suffers loss as a result. Section 3-605 is concerned with this kind of problem with 
Principal Debtor and Surety. But it has a wider scope: it also applies to indorsers who are not

qa_pairs.question: Under what circumstances is the obligation of an indorser or accommodation party discharged when the holder agrees to an extension of the due date of the obligation of the obligor?
qa_pairs.answer: The obligation of an indorser or accommodation party is discharged when the holder agrees to an extension of the due date of the obligation of the obligor, to the extent that the indorser or accommodation party can prove that the extension caused her loss with respect to her right of recourse against the obligor. This means that if the extension of the due date results in a financial loss for the indorser or accommodation party, their obligation to the holder is discharged.

qa_pairs.question: How does a material modification of the obligor's obligation, other than an extension of the due date, affect the obligation of an indorser or accommodation party having a right of recourse against the obligor?
qa_pairs.answer: A material modification of the obligor's obligation, other than an extension of the due date, discharges the obligation of an indorser or accommodation party having a right of recourse against the obligor to the extent that the modification causes her loss with respect to her right of recourse. This means that if the holder makes significant changes to the terms of the obligor's obligation that result in a financial loss for the indorser or accommodation party, their obligation to the holder is discharged.

Discharge by Reacquisition 
Suppose a prior party reacquires the instrument. He may—but does not automatically—cancel any 
indorsement unnecessary to his title and may also reissue or further negotiate the instrument. Any 
intervening party is thereby discharged from liability to the reacquiring party or to any subsequent holder 
not in due course. If an intervening party’s indorsement is cancelled, she is not liable even to an HDC. [5] 
Discharge by Unexcused Delay in Presentment or Notice of Dishonor 
If notice of dishonor is not excused under UCC Section 3-504, failure to give it discharges drawers and 
indorsers. 
 
KEY TAKEAWAY 
 
The potential liabilities arising from commercial paper are discharged in several ways. Anything that would 
discharge a debt under common contract law will do so. More specifically as to commercial paper, of course, 
payment discharges the obligation. Other methods include tender of payment, cancellation or renunciation, 
material and fraudulent alteration, certification, acceptance varying a draft, reacquisition, and—in some 
cases—unexcused delay in giving notice of presentment or dishonor. Indorsers and accommodation parties’ 
liability may be discharged by the same means that a surety’s liability is discharged, to the extent that 
alterations in the agreement between the creditor and the holder would be defenses to a surety because right 
of recourse is impaired to the surety.

qa_pairs.question: What is the most common way that obligations represented by commercial paper are discharged?
qa_pairs.answer: The most common way that obligations represented by commercial paper are discharged is through payment. When a debtor makes a payment to the holder of the commercial paper, it fulfills the obligation and discharges the debt. This is a fundamental principle in commercial transactions, as it provides a clear and straightforward method for settling debts. Payment can be made in various forms, such as cash, check, or electronic transfer, and it must be made to the holder of the instrument. Once the payment is made, the debtor is no longer liable for the debt represented by the commercial paper, and the obligation is considered satisfied.

qa_pairs.question: If Parents ceremoniously tear up the promissory note given by Daughter at her graduation party, is Daughter's obligation terminated?
qa_pairs.answer: No, Daughter's obligation is not terminated if Parents ceremoniously tear up the promissory note. The act of tearing up the note does not constitute a legal discharge of the obligation under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) or common contract law. For the obligation to be legally discharged, there must be a valid discharge of the debt, such as payment, tender of payment, cancellation or renunciation, material and fraudulent alteration, certification, acceptance varying a draft, reacquisition, or in some cases, unexcused delay in giving notice of presentment or dishonor. Simply tearing up the note does not meet any of these criteria and therefore does not legally terminate the obligation. Daughter remains liable for the debt represented by the promissory note unless one of the other methods of discharge is applied.

qa_pairs.question: What is the most common way that obligations represented by commercial paper are discharged?
qa_pairs.answer: The most common way that obligations represented by commercial paper are discharged is through payment. When the holder of the commercial paper presents it for payment, and the maker or acceptor of the paper pays the amount due, the obligation is considered discharged. This method of discharge is straightforward and is the primary means by which commercial paper obligations are settled. In some cases, the obligation may also be discharged through other means such as cancellation, where the parties involved agree to terminate the obligation, or through the loss of the paper, where the holder loses possession of the paper and cannot enforce it.

qa_pairs.question: Is Daughter’s obligation terminated when Parents ceremoniously tear up the promissory note at her graduation party?
qa_pairs.answer: No, Daughter's obligation is not terminated when Parents ceremoniously tear up the promissory note at her graduation party. The act of tearing up the note does not constitute a legal discharge of the obligation under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC). According to UCC Section 3-604, a discharge of an obligation represented by a negotiable instrument requires an explicit agreement between the parties or a legal action that results in the discharge. Simply tearing up the note does not meet these criteria. qa_pairs.question: How did BOK breach its presentment warranty to BNH?
qa_pairs.answer: BOK breached its presentment warranty to BNH by failing to present the check for payment in a timely manner. According to the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) § 3-501, a presentment warranty is made when a person presents a negotiable instrument for payment or acceptance. qa_pairs.question: In what way was Farm Bureau Mutual Insurance Co. negligent in this case, and what was the consequence?
qa_pairs.answer: Farm Bureau Mutual Insurance Co. was negligent in this case by failing to notify the mortgagee, BOK, about a significant loss. According to the UCC § 3-406, a party's negligence substantially contributing to the forgery of an instrument can be considered negligence. In this case, Farm Bureau issued a loss check to the insured without notifying BOK, which is a standard practice in the industry to avoid such situations. BOK's expert testified that it is standard practice in the industry to notify the lender of a loss this size. The trial court concluded that Farm Bureau did not act in a commercially reasonable manner and that this failure was negligence which substantially contributed to the forgery. qa_pairs.question: What is the significance of a bank's acceptance of a check according to § 3-409 and § 3-413?
qa_pairs.answer: The significance of a bank's acceptance of a check, as outlined in § 3-409 and § 3-413, lies in the bank's obligation to pay the check. According to § 3-409, acceptance of a check becomes effective when the presenter is notified of that fact. This means that the bank must communicate to the presenter that it will honor the check. Once accepted, under § 3-413, the bank is then obligated to pay the check. In the context of the provided text, the bank's acceptance of the check is crucial because it determines whether the bank has a duty to pay the check. If the bank does not accept the check, it is not obligated to pay, regardless of any other circumstances. This is why the bank's refusal to pay the check in the given scenario was not considered dishonor under § 3-502, as the bank never accepted the check.

qa_pairs.question: Why did the intermediate appellate court find that there was no acceptance of the check by the Bank?
qa_pairs.answer: The intermediate appellate court found that there was no acceptance of the check by the Bank because the Bank never communicated to the Petitioner that it would honor the check. The facts demonstrated that the Bank's teller and branch manager informed the Petitioner that it was against bank policy to honor the check without a thumbprint signature. The court concluded that the Bank's refusal to pay the check did not constitute dishonor under § 3-502 because the Bank never accepted the check.

qa_pairs.question: What is the significance of the Bank of America's Thumbprint Signature Program in the context of the case discussed in the text segment?
qa_pairs.answer: The Bank of America's Thumbprint Signature Program is central to the case as it pertains to the issue of whether requiring a thumbprint constitutes 'reasonable identification' under § 3-501(b)(2)(ii) of the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC). The Bank argues that its contractual relationship with its customer, the drawer, authorizes the use of this program as a reasonable form of identification. This argument is based on the premise that the contractual agreement between the Bank and its customer allows the Bank to refuse to accept checks that do not comply with the Thumbprint Signature Program, without dishonoring the check as per § 3-501(b)(3)(ii). The Bank contends that its refusal to accept the check in this case was based on the presentment failing to comply with 'an agreement of the parties,' which is the contract between the Bank and its customer. However, the intermediate appellate court agreed with the Bank, but the higher court disagreed, stating that the contract between the Bank and its customer does not apply to Petitioner and does not give him a cause of action against the Bank. The higher court also emphasized that the determination of what constitutes 'reasonable identification' is a broader policy consideration and not merely a matter of contract. Therefore, the Thumbprint Signature Program's role in this case is to test the boundaries of what is considered 'reasonable identification' under the UCC and to explore whether contractual agreements between banks and their customers can dictate the terms of presentment and acceptance of checks.

qa_pairs.question: Why did the higher court disagree with the intermediate appellate court's decision regarding the Bank of America's Thumbprint Signature Program?
qa_pairs.answer: The higher court disagreed with the intermediate appellate court's decision because it believed that the contract between the Bank and its customer does not apply to Petitioner and does not give him a cause of action against the Bank. The higher court also argued that the determination of what constitutes 'reasonable identification' under § 3-501(b)(2)(ii) is a broader policy consideration, not simply a matter of contract. The higher court emphasized that the Bank's contractual agreement with its customer cannot define the meaning of 'reasonable identification' and impose it upon parties who are not in privity with that contract. Therefore, the higher court concluded that requiring a thumbprint does not constitute 'reasonable identification' under the UCC, and the Bank's refusal to accept the check may constitute dishonor under § 3-502(b)(2). The higher court's disagreement highlights the tension between contractual agreements between banks and their customers and the broader policy considerations of the UCC.

qa_pairs.question: Why do banks assume the risk when cashing checks over the counter, and what are the potential consequences of this risk?
qa_pairs.answer: Banks assume the risk when cashing checks over the counter because they are required to provide certain warranties, such as the payee's entitlement to enforce the instrument and the absence of alterations on the check. These warranties cannot be disclaimed, and if breached, the bank may suffer losses. The potential consequences of this risk include the bank incurring expenses to find the presenter, demand repayment, and legal costs to pursue the presenter for breach of warranties. The Commercial Law Article does not force banks to assume these risks, but their willingness to cash checks over the counter with reasonable identification expands and facilitates commercial activities within the state. By accepting this risk, banks play a crucial role in the smooth functioning of commerce, despite the potential for financial loss due to counterfeit documents, forged endorsements, or altered checks.

qa_pairs.question: What does Section 4-208 of the Uniform Commercial Code stipulate regarding the presentation of an unaccepted draft and the warranties provided by the person obtaining payment or acceptance and a previous transferor of the draft?
qa_pairs.answer: Section 4-208 of the Uniform Commercial Code outlines the warranties that must be provided when an unaccepted draft is presented for payment or acceptance. Specifically, it states that if a person obtains payment or acceptance of an unaccepted draft, they must warrant to the drawee that: (1) they are, or were, at the time of transfer, a person entitled to enforce the draft or authorized to obtain payment or acceptance on behalf of a person entitled to enforce the draft; (2) the draft has not been altered; and (3) the warrantor has no knowledge that the signature of the purported drawer of the draft is unauthorized. Additionally, if the drawee makes payment, they may recover damages from the warrantor for breach of warranty. The drawee can also assert a claim for breach of warranty based on an unauthorized indorsement or alteration of the draft, and the warrantor may defend by proving that the drawer is precluded from asserting against the drawee the unauthorized indorsement or alteration under Section 3-406 or 4-406 of the title.

qa_pairs.question: How does Section 3-406 of the Uniform Commercial Code relate to a person's failure to exercise ordinary care and the assertion of alteration or forgery against a person who pays the instrument in good faith?
qa_pairs.answer: Section 3-406 of the Uniform Commercial Code addresses the issue of a person's failure to exercise ordinary care and its impact on the assertion of alteration or forgery against a person who pays the instrument in good faith. It states that a person whose failure to exercise ordinary care substantially contributes to an alteration of an instrument or to the making of a forged signature on an instrument is precluded from asserting the alteration or the forgery against a person who, in good faith, pays the instrument or takes it for value or for collection. This means that if a person's negligence or lack of ordinary care leads to the alteration or forgery of an instrument, they cannot later claim that the instrument was altered or forged against a good faith payer. The person asserting preclusion may, however, be held partially liable under comparative negligence principles for failing to exercise ordinary care in paying or taking the check. This provision aims to encourage individuals and entities to exercise due diligence in handling financial instruments to prevent fraud and forgery.

22.6 Summary and Exercises 
 
Summary 
As a general rule, one who signs a note as maker or a draft as drawer is personally liable unless he or she 
signs in a representative capacity and either the instrument or the signature shows that the signing has 
been made in a representative capacity. Various rules govern the permutations of signatures when an 
agent and a principal are involved. 
 
The maker of a note and the acceptor of a draft have primary contract liability on the instruments. 
Secondarily liable are drawers and indorsers. Conditions precedent to secondary liability are presentment, 
dishonor, and notice of dishonor. Under the proper circumstances, any of these conditions may be waived 
or excused. 
 
Presentment is a demand for payment made on the maker, acceptor, or drawee, or a demand for 
acceptance on the drawee. Presentment must be made (1) at the time specified in the instrument unless 
no time is specified, in which case it must be at the time specified for payment, or (2) within a reasonable 
time if a sight instrument. 
 
Dishonor occurs when acceptance or payment is refused after presentment, at which time a holder has the 
right of recourse against secondary parties if he has given proper notice of dishonor. 
 
A seller-transferor of any commercial paper gives five implied warranties, which become valuable to a 
holder seeking to collect in the event that there has been no indorsement or the indorsement has been 
qualified. These warranties are (1) good title, (2) genuine signatures, (3) no material alteration, (4) no

maker, acceptor, or drawer. 
A holder on presentment makes certain warranties also: (1) entitled to enforce the instrument, (2) no 
knowledge that the maker’s or drawer’s signature is unauthorized, and (3) no material alteration.

qa_pairs.question: What are the conditions precedent to secondary liability for drawers and indorsers in the context of commercial paper?
qa_pairs.answer: The conditions precedent to secondary liability for drawers and indorsers in the context of commercial paper are presentment, dishonor, and notice of dishonor. Presentment is a demand for payment made on the maker, acceptor, or drawee, or a demand for acceptance on the drawee, and must be made at the specified time or within a reasonable time if the instrument is a sight instrument. Dishonor occurs when acceptance or payment is refused after presentment, at which point a holder has the right of recourse against secondary parties if proper notice of dishonor has been given. Notice of dishonor is a formal notification to the secondary parties that the instrument has been dishonored, which is necessary for them to be held liable.

qa_pairs.question: What are the five implied warranties given by a seller-transferor of commercial paper to a holder seeking to collect?
qa_pairs.answer: The five implied warranties given by a seller-transferor of commercial paper to a holder seeking to collect are: (1) Good title, meaning the transferor has the right to transfer the instrument and the title to the instrument is valid and enforceable. (2) Genuine signatures, indicating that the signatures on the instrument are authentic and not forged. (3) No material alteration, which means that the instrument has not been altered in any way that would affect the rights and obligations of the parties involved. (4) No defenses by other parties to the obligation to pay the transferor, implying that there are no valid defenses that other parties can raise against the transferor's right to collect on the instrument. (5) No knowledge of insolvency of the maker, acceptor, or drawer, meaning that the transferor was not aware of the financial instability or insolvency of these parties at the time of the transfer.

qa_pairs.answer: In the scenario where Robb stole a blank check, forged Markum's signature, and cashed it at Friendly Check Cashing Company, which then deposited it with Farmer’s National, the loss will likely be borne by Farmer’s National. This is because Farmer’s National, as the drawee bank, is responsible for verifying the authenticity of the check before processing it. However, since the theft and forgery were quickly discovered by Markum, who promptly notified Unity, Unity may also bear some responsibility for not detecting the forgery sooner. The exact allocation of loss between Farmer’s National and Unity would depend on the specific terms of their agreement and the applicable laws governing such transactions. In general, banks are expected to exercise due diligence in verifying checks, but they may also be held liable if they fail to do so. Unity, as the payee, may also bear some responsibility if it is found that they did not take adequate steps to prevent such fraud.

qa_pairs.question: In the case where Pat stole a check made out to Marks, forged Marks' name, and negotiated it to Harrison for cash, who will bear the loss when Central County Bank paid the check without knowing about the theft or forgery?
qa_pairs.answer: In the case where Pat stole a check made out to Marks, forged Marks' name, and negotiated it to Harrison for cash, Central County Bank, the drawee bank, will bear the loss. This is because Central County Bank is responsible for verifying the authenticity of the check before processing it. When Pat presented the forged check for payment, Central County Bank failed to exercise due diligence in verifying the check, which led to the payment being made to Pat instead of Marks. As a result, Central County Bank is liable for the loss incurred by Marks due to the forged check. Pat, who committed the theft and forgery, may also be held personally liable for the loss, but the primary responsibility lies with Central County Bank for failing to detect the forgery and process the check correctly.

qa_pairs.question: What is the legal outcome when a bank pays out on altered checks, as in the case of Baker who altered the amount of checks and cashed them at First Bank?
qa_pairs.answer: In the case of Baker who altered the amount of checks and cashed them at First Bank, the legal outcome is that Baker was sent to prison for the fraud committed. Able, the victim of the fraud, sued First Bank for paying out on the altered instruments. qa_pairs.question: What is the liability of Juanita, Christina Reynolds' sister, who signed the note as an accommodation maker for Christina's loan from First Bank?
qa_pairs.answer: Juanita, Christina Reynolds' sister, who signed the note as an accommodation maker for Christina's loan from First Bank, has secondary liability. This means that she is only liable if Christina, the primary obligor, defaults on the loan. In this case, when Christina failed to complete payment on the note for the Ford, Bank turned to Juanita for payment. Therefore, Juanita is liable for the debt, but only after Christina has defaulted and the bank has exhausted all other means of collection.

qa_pairs.question: What is the primary focus of Article 4 of the UCC in relation to banking operations?
qa_pairs.answer: Article 4 of the UCC primarily focuses on the relationship between banks and their customers, specifically governing the operations of the banking system with respect to its depositors and customers. It deals with bank deposits and collections, including the traditional bank collection process for checks. This article is state-based and applies to the daily operations of checking accounts, ensuring that the rules governing these processes are consistent and regulated at the state level. qa_pairs.question: How has the Electronic Fund Transfer Act impacted the banking industry?
qa_pairs.answer: The Electronic Fund Transfer Act has significantly impacted the banking industry by addressing the rise of non-check banking and the increasing use of electronic payment methods. This federal law governs the electronic transfer of funds, ensuring consumer protection and establishing the rights and liabilities of parties involved in electronic fund transfers. The Act has facilitated the growth of electronic banking services, such as online banking, debit and credit card transactions, and prepaid cards, by providing a legal framework that promotes security, reliability, and consumer confidence in electronic transactions. As a result, the banking industry has adapted to these changes, offering a wider range of payment instruments to consumers and enhancing the overall efficiency and convenience of financial transactions.

qa_pairs.question: What is the traditional check-collection process and what are the roles of the different banks involved according to the provided text?
qa_pairs.answer: The traditional check-collection process involves a series of banks handling a check from the moment it is written until it is returned to the payor bank. The bank upon which a check is written is known as the payor bank, also referred to as the drawee bank. The bank where the check is deposited by the payee is called the depository bank. Throughout the process, various banks are involved, including collecting banks and intermediary banks. Collecting banks are all the banks that handle the check except for the payor and depository banks. Intermediary banks are the collecting banks except for the payor and depository banks. For example, if Roger in Seattle writes a check on his account at Seattle Bank and mails it to Julia in Los Angeles, Bank of L.A. in Los Angeles acts as both a depository bank and a collecting bank. Any other bank through which the check travels, except for the payor bank (Seattle Bank) and the depository bank (Bank of L.A.), would be considered an intermediary bank. This complex process ensures that the check is properly routed and eventually returned to the payor bank.

If the depository bank is also the payor bank (about 30% of all checks), the check is called an “on-us” item 
and UCC 4-215(e)(2) provides that—if the check is not dishonored—it is available by the payee “at the

both of whom have accounts at Seattle Bank; Matthew deposits the check on Monday. On Wednesday the 
check is good for Matthew (he may have been given “provisional credit” before then, as discussed below, 
the bank could subtract the money from his account if Roger didn’t have enough to cover the check). 
 
Collection Process between Customers of Different Banks 
Roger in Seattle writes a check on Seattle Bank payable to Julia in L.A. Julia deposits it in her account at 
L.A. Bank, the depository bank. L.A. Bank must somehow present the check to Seattle Bank either directly 
or through intermediary banks. If the collecting banks (again, all of them except Seattle Bank) act before 
the midnight deadline following receipt, they have acted “seasonably” according to UCC 4-202. When the 
payor bank—Seattle Bank—gets the check it must pay it, unless the check is dishonored or returned (UCC 
4-302).

qa_pairs.question: What is the role of a depository bank in the check collection process between customers of different banks?
qa_pairs.answer: In the check collection process between customers of different banks, a depository bank is the bank where the payee deposits the check. For example, if Roger in Seattle writes a check payable to Julia in Los Angeles, Julia deposits the check in her account at Bank of L.A., which acts as the depository bank. The depository bank is responsible for presenting the check to the payor bank, which in this case is Seattle Bank. The depository bank may present the check directly to Seattle Bank or through intermediary banks. The depository bank must act seasonably, meaning it must present the check to the payor bank before the midnight deadline following receipt, as per UCC 4-202. Once the check is presented, Seattle Bank is obligated to pay the check unless it is dishonored or returned, according to UCC 4-302.

qa_pairs.question: What is an 'on-us' item in the context of check collection, and how does it differ from a check that travels through intermediary banks?
qa_pairs.answer: 'An on-us' item refers to a check that is deposited by a customer into their own bank account, where the bank is also the payor bank. In the context of check collection, if the depository bank is the same as the payor bank, the check is considered an 'on-us' item. For instance, if Roger writes a check to Matthew, and both Roger and Matthew have accounts at Seattle Bank, the check is an 'on-us' item. According to UCC 4-215(e)(2), if the check is not dishonored, it is available to the payee 'at the opening of the bank’s second banking day following receipt of the item.' This means that Matthew can access the funds from the check on the second banking day after depositing it, without the need for the check to travel through intermediary banks. In contrast, a check that travels through intermediary banks is not an 'on-us' item. This type of check involves the depository bank presenting the check to the payor bank through one or more intermediary banks. The check must be presented seasonably, and the payor bank is obligated to pay the check unless it is dishonored or returned, as per UCC 4-302. The key difference is that 'on-us' items are processed within the same bank, while checks that travel through intermediary banks involve multiple banks in the collection process.

qa_pairs.question: What is the effect of a 'pay any bank' indorsement on a check?
qa_pairs.answer: The effect of a 'pay any bank' indorsement on a check is significant in the context of bank transactions. When the words 'pay any bank' are indorsed on a check, it restricts the rights of the holder to only banks. This means that only a bank can acquire the rights of a holder of the check. However, this restriction can be lifted under two specific conditions. Firstly, the restriction can be lifted if the check has been returned to the customer who initiated the collection. In such a case, the check can be indorsed to a non-bank entity. Secondly, the restriction can be lifted if the bank itself specially indorses the check to a person who is not a bank. This indorsement by the bank effectively removes the restriction, allowing the check to be transferred to a non-bank holder. This provision ensures flexibility in the handling of checks and facilitates the transfer of rights to non-bank entities under certain circumstances.

qa_pairs.question: Are any warranties given in the collection process, and if so, what are they?
qa_pairs.answer: Yes, warranties are given in the collection process, and they are identical to those provided in Article 3, except that they apply only to customers and collecting banks. These warranties are crucial in ensuring the integrity and trustworthiness of the collection process. The warranties provided in the collection process include several key assurances. Firstly, the customer or collecting bank that transfers an item and receives a settlement or other consideration warrants that they are entitled to enforce the item. This means that the customer or bank has the legal right to demand payment from the party obligated to pay the instrument. Secondly, they warrant that all signatures on the instrument are authorized and authentic. This ensures that the signatures are genuine and that the parties involved have the authority to sign the instrument. Thirdly, they warrant that the item has not been altered in any way. This assurance is critical in maintaining the integrity of the instrument and preventing fraud. Fourthly, they warrant that the item is not subject to any defense or claim in recoupment. This means that the item is free from any legal defenses or claims that could be raised by the obligor to avoid payment. Lastly, they warrant that they have no knowledge of any insolvency proceedings regarding the maker or acceptor, or in the case of an unaccepted draft, the drawer. This ensures that the customer or bank is not aware of any financial instability or legal proceedings that could affect the payment of the instrument. These warranties cannot be disclaimed as to checks, ensuring a high level of protection for all parties involved in the collection process.

Common Issues Arising between Banks and Their Customers 
Payment of Overdrafts 
Suppose a customer writes a check for a sum greater than the amount in her account. May the bank pay 
the check and charge the customer’s account? Under Section 4-401(1), it may. Moreover, it may pay on an 
altered check and charge the customer’s account for the original tenor of the check, and if a check was 
completed it may pay the completed amount and charge the customer’s account, assuming the bank acted 
in good faith without knowledge that the completion was improper. 
 
Payment of Stale Checks 
Section 4-404 permits a bank to refuse to pay a check that was drawn more than six months before being 
presented. Banks ordinarily consider such checks to be “stale” and will refuse to pay them, but the same 
section gives them the option to pay if they choose. A corporate dividend check, for example, will be 
presumed to be good more than six months later. The only exception to this rule is for certified checks, 
which must be paid whenever presented, since the customer’s account was charged when the check was 
certified.

qa_pairs.question: Under Section 4-401(1), may a bank pay a check for an amount greater than the customer's account balance, and if so, under what conditions?
qa_pairs.answer: Yes, under Section 4-401(1), a bank may pay a check for an amount greater than the customer's account balance. This is known as paying an overdraft. The bank may charge the customer's account for the overdraft amount. However, the bank must act in good faith and without knowledge that the completion of the check was improper. This means that the bank should not have any reason to suspect that the check was altered or completed in a fraudulent manner. If the bank pays the check and charges the customer's account for the overdraft, it is entitled to recover the overdraft amount from the customer, even if the customer disputes the charge.

qa_pairs.question: What are the conditions under which a bank may refuse to pay a stale check, and are there any exceptions to this rule?
qa_pairs.answer: Under Section 4-404, a bank may refuse to pay a check that was drawn more than six months before being presented, as such checks are considered 'stale'. However, banks have the option to pay stale checks if they choose. An exception to this rule is for certified checks, which must be paid whenever presented. This is because the customer's account was charged when the check was certified, and the bank has a duty to honor the certification. Another exception is for corporate dividend checks, which are presumed to be good more than six months after being drawn, as they are considered to be in the ordinary course of business.

An oral stop order is effective for fourteen days; a follow-up written confirmation within that time is 
effective for six months and can be renewed in writing. But if a stop order is not renewed, the bank will 
not be liable for paying the check, even one that is quite stale (e.g., Granite Equipment Leasing Corp. v. 
Hempstead Bank, 326 N.Y.S. 2d 881 (1971)). 
 
Wrongful Dishonor 
If a bank wrongfully dishonors an item, it is liable to the customer for all damages that are a direct 
consequence of (“proximately caused by”) the dishonor. The bank’s liability is limited to the damages 
actually proved; these may include damages for arrest and prosecution. See Section 23.4 "Cases" under 
“Bank’s Liability for Paying over Customer’s ‘Stop Payment’ Order” (Meade v. National Bank of Adams 
County). 
 
Customers’ Duties 
In order to hold a bank liable for paying out an altered check, the customer has certain duties under 
Section 4-406. Primarily, the customer must act promptly in examining her statement of account and 
must notify the bank if any check has been altered or her signature has been forged. If the customer fails

it suffered a loss because of the customer’s slowness. Recovery may also be denied when there has been a 
series of forgeries and the customer did not notify the bank within two weeks after receiving the first 
forged item. See Section 23.4 "Cases" under “Customer’s Duty to Inspect Bank Statements” (the Planters 
Bank v. Rogers case). 
 
These rules apply to a payment made with ordinary care by the bank. If the customer can show that the 
bank negligently paid the item, then the customer may recover from the bank, regardless of how dilatory 
the customer was in notifying the bank—with two exceptions: (1) from the time she first sees the 
statement and item, the customer has one year to tell the bank that her signature was unauthorized or 
that a term was altered, and (2) she has three years to report an unauthorized indorsement.
